Install the latest available Forever file from [CurseForge](https://www.curseforge.com/wow/addons/flourishforever). Version `0.4.3-beta` is prepared but has not yet been confirmed there. The game addon directory `_forever_/Interface/AddOns/FlourishForever/` must contain `FlourishForever.toc`, `FlourishForever_Storage.lua`, `FlourishForever.lua`, and `FlourishForever_ActionEmotes.lua`.

Settings persist in `FlourishForeverStorage`, indexed by character GUID. Older boolean emote selections are migrated; in the **unreleased cooldown fix**, per-emote last-fired timestamps also persist across `/reload` and relog, while the in-session clock retains precise timing.

## The rhythm of a chosen expression — approved November 7 design

Each ability may have several possible emotes, each with a different **cooldown duration**. Once one is randomly chosen, that duration pauses **all flourishes on that ability**. A small gesture can leave room for another expression after three seconds; a powerful gesture can set a twenty-second silence before the next one. The ability's chance and chosen trigger mode remain independent controls, and no other configured ability is affected.

This replaces the earlier independent per-emote eligibility model, where different emotes could trigger during each other's cooldown. The individual sliders remain; only the effect of the chosen timer changes. Babuni confirmed the older timers were working before approving this refinement. The revised model is implemented, automatically tested, and was reported working in the actual Forever client by Babuni on 7 November 2026. Battleground and exhaustive trigger-security testing remain open.

## A flourish of personality at the moment of action

Combat abilities can be mechanically identical every time they are used, while the character using them may have a very different personality. **Flourish Forever** links ordinary, player-chosen ability casts to an expressive action: an in-game emote. A Warrior's moment of aggression might produce a roar; another chosen spell might draw from entirely different gestures. The goal is **atmosphere and character expression**, not a gameplay advantage.

The creative requirement is choice. The player decides *which* abilities deserve a flourish, *which* emotes may accompany them, *how often* the response is allowed, and whether the system is active on this character at all. The addon must not force an unsolicited global roleplay persona onto other characters or every spell in the spellbook.

The October 22 creative discussion described the idea in terms of **automatic random emotes for selected abilities**. The updated implementation extends that principle with a searchable, categorized spellbook interface, a master switch, a curated spell list, per-ability chance, and individually adjustable emote cooldown durations that lock the whole configured ability when chosen. The portfolio record credits Babuni's human direction without retroactively assigning its conception to an assistant.

## Timing belongs to the player

The original desired behavior remains the default: a flourish follows a **successful cast**, not merely a button press. Babuni also approved Button press and Failure as explicit per-ability timing choices beside the Chance control. This lets a Warrior's shout feel different from a spell that fizzles or an impatient gesture that comes before the action.

Success uses the player's own cast-success report; Failure uses failed or interrupted cast events; Button press uses the player-action hook. A battleground/arena temporarily switches the default Success mode to Button press to avoid the previously observed protected native-emote callback, provided chat is not locked down. It never changes the saved preference.

Forever's restrictions differ for native emotes and custom chat. Player-authored `/e` text requires direct input and cannot be promised on a later success/failure event. The implementation must say so in the editor rather than silently breaking protected-chat rules. The chosen emote pool, chance, cooldown, character identity and user agency remain unchanged.
## Variation without noise

An emote on every cast may become repetitive or irritating. The design gives each ability its own **0–100% probability** while each selected emote has its own **0–120-second cooldown**. A dramatic gesture can impose a longer silence on its ability than a small gesture, while the next emote remains a random choice after that lock expires.

Once a configured cast passes those checks, the program chooses uniformly from the enabled emote tokens. The player can select a single reliable signature gesture or a larger pool for surprise. **ROAR** is the default *allowed emote* when a spell is first added; it is not a hardcoded requirement, and the default ability list is empty.

The expanded editor offers both the game's native emote-token vocabulary and player-written `/e` lines. The latter are ordinary chat emotes, not custom animations or new sound files. In the public version, native emotes are attempted after cast-success and custom text during the player's button press. The experimental security fix instead triggers both on a real action press, with the possibility of emotes on failed casts. Babuni reported the revised behavior working as before and requested the patch; the failed-cast timing trade-off is documented.

## Honor the boundaries of player agency

Originally the native-emote trigger was the player's **reported successful spellcast event**, not an actual hit. Custom text is generated at the button press. The experimental 0.4.1-beta-dev implementation attempts both emote types on user action instead, never automatically casts a spell, and remains subject to Forever's security restrictions. The timing change is prepared for release following the positive general in-game report; the original cast-success version remains part of the recorded history.

Character settings are isolated by **character GUID**, consistent with the realmless Forever naming environment. The existing source contains migration logic for previously name-keyed profiles, but the full historical ROARitFOREVER design conversation isn't present in the inspected Git repository. That conditional migration path isn't evidence a separate realm model applies.

## Why this small concept makes a useful portfolio piece

The interaction is an example of **emergent personality made from a few small systems**: a player-chosen ability action, a probability decision, a time limit, a curated list and a user interface. The computer contributes variation; the player contributes taste and character identity.

The difference from an always-on automated announcer is essential. The player can curate or remove any configured spell, leave some abilities entirely untouched, disable the system without deleting settings, or uncheck every emote to make one configuration silent.

The expanded searchable interface and custom text were recovered from Babuni's earlier development archive and approved for integration. Other ideas, such as emote previews or global spam control, remain proposals rather than implemented features. They remain choices for Babuni after real in-game testing.

## Related development history

Flourish Forever is the October 2026 WoW Forever expression of the action-emote idea. Unlike the earlier action-slot hooks, it responds to the player’s **reported successful spellcast** event and lets the player select spellbook abilities and existing client-native emotes in a GUI. Each new ability initially has ROAR selected, but the player may choose other available emote tokens. This is client-token selection rather than creation of arbitrary new emotes, and cast success does not prove a landed hit. ## Making ability casts feel like character moments

Flourish Forever belongs to a particular thread of my experiments: allowing a character to do more than mechanically repeat a combat ability. A player may associate an important attack with a roar, a cheer, a gesture or a sudden burst of personality. But the game normally presents the ability as a spell and its ordinary combat animation, without adding this small expressive choice.

The idea was to make **automatic random emotes on selected abilities** possible. That small phrase captures the concept: not a system that chooses what the character casts, not a macro that must be pressed separately every time, and not a scripted roleplay monologue that speaks for the player without limits. A configured combat action becomes an opportunity for a tiny, variable flourish.

The public repository describes it as allowing the player to pick abilities from the spellbook, then set an independent chance, a cooldown and the emotes that might appear. The program expresses that in a way which leaves taste with the player. A powerful defensive ability might rarely produce one emblematic gesture, while a different move has a small menu of possible actions. The random choice introduces surprise but the source of variation remains the player's own selection.

As Babuni, the original creative direction is mine. The available material does not provide a full original ideation transcript, exact rejected names or whether a particular coding assistant typed each October 22 Lua function. The October 27 documentation assistant is recording source and conversation evidence, not claiming to have originated the concept.

## October 22, 2026 — a first Git commit that already contains a full interface

The first repository commit, **`b60d08024cdd`**, carries the message “Ship Flourish Forever 0.3.0-beta with configurable ability emotes.” There is no preceding 0.1 or 0.2 commit in this particular Git history. The first visible state is already a working-intent addon with a three-part source structure and a Blizzard-style configuration window.

One module, **FlourishForever_Storage.lua**, manages account-wide SavedVariables and individual character profiles. A second, **FlourishForever.lua**, routes slash commands. The largest module, **FlourishForever_ActionEmotes.lua**, discovers eligible spells and emote tokens, creates the editor, processes the chance/cooldown logic and listens for cast-success events.

The TOC sets **interface 16001**, declares `FlourishForeverStorage` and loads those three modules in that order. The repo's `.pkgmeta` indicates an intent to package the addon as FlourishForever with a manual changelog.

The first source already had a crucial autonomy detail: **every character gets its own choices**. The account-wide SavedVariables root is divided into profiles indexed by `UnitGUID("player")`, not by a name which might be ambiguous or by a set of separate realms. In World of Warcraft: Forever's relevant identity model there are **no separate realms**. The presence of optional older name-realm keys in migration code simply preserves an earlier storage format; it does not introduce cross-realm behavior.

The config defaults to **enabled** for the current character, but the ability list starts empty. That means the addon does not begin roaring on its own merely because it is installed. The player selects an actual spellbook ability first. This is a better creative fit than globally hooking every spell without asking: the character's expressive habits are authored through configuration.

## Building a controllable moment rather than an uncontrolled reflex

The configuration window is about **620×520 pixels** and uses the game's own inset frame, buttons, checkboxes, sliders and scroll surfaces. The player opens it through `/flourish`, chooses a non-passive ability from the spellbook dropdown, then sees configured abilities on the left and the selected one's options on the right.

Chance runs from **0 to 100 percent** in 1% steps and defaults to **100%** for a newly added spell. Cooldown runs from **0 to 120 seconds** and defaults to **six seconds**. Each configured spell starts with **ROAR** enabled as its possible emote, but the player can check other emotes from the client-provided emote list or uncheck ROAR entirely.

The collection of available emotes comes from the client's global `EMOTE*_TOKEN` values, not from a hand-written list of three or four favorite animations. The source sorts and labels those tokens, using `GetEmoteSlashCmd` when the client provides it. If no checkbox is selected for one spell, there is no valid outcome for that spell and the addon stays silent.

At runtime, the addon listens for **UNIT_SPELLCAST_SUCCEEDED** for the player. It resolves the spell ID into a spell name, finds a configuration for the lowercase/trimmed name, checks the ability's last-played emote timestamp, rolls the configured probability and randomly selects a permitted token. It then calls **DoEmote**. Importantly, the local timestamp is updated **only after a token is chosen**, so a failed chance roll doesn't consume an otherwise available cooldown.

This sequence is simple enough to describe in one paragraph, but it combines several decisions with a meaningful effect on the player's experience. A 20% chance is not “every fifth cast”; it may trigger twice in a row or remain silent for longer. A cooldown is not the game spell cooldown; it is a minimum time since this ability's previous flourish. The two controls shape a rhythm without giving the program control of the combat rotation.

## What “successful” means—and why that distinction matters

The initial prose described the feature as an emote appearing when an ability “lands.” Source review reveals that the code does **not** inspect combat-log hits or the eventual effect on a target. It responds when the game announces that the **spellcast succeeded**. A spell could be cast successfully while its damage later misses or is resisted, or its target effect doesn't occur the way the player expected.

This isn't necessarily a mistake; choosing cast-success events is a reasonable way to capture a broad range of combat and utility actions without complicated hit correlation. But it is a semantic difference the README must not conceal. The documentation now calls it *cast success*, and marks any proposal to switch to landed-hit triggers as **undecided**.

Another static finding is the first-cast timer. `lastFireByAbility[key]` begins absent and falls back to the number **0**. On a very early cast, if `GetTime()` has advanced less than the configured six-second cooldown, the expression `now - last < cooldown` is true and prevents that emote. The audit hasn't reproduced the event in-game; the code path makes it a plausible edge case worth testing.

The source also stores its current spell configuration under a **normalized ability name**, though it receives actual spell IDs from the event and dropdown. This can conveniently unify ranks whose names match, but may confuse players who see distinct spellbook entries with the same name. Localized spell-name changes can also make a saved configuration stop matching. These risks deserve targeted tests rather than an assumption of universal compatibility.

## Profiles, older names and the importance of not losing choices

The storage module includes two backward-compatibility mechanisms. If the current `FlourishForeverStorage` root is absent and an old **ROARitFOREVERStorage** global is already loaded, it adopts that data. Then, if the current character's GUID profile is missing, it looks for a profile stored under the plain character name or a legacy name-realm-style key and moves that table to the GUID key.

The intent visible in code is preserving previous character choices rather than discarding them during a rename or identity-model change. The availability of that old global isn't guaranteed by simply installing the newer addon: the current TOC loads only `FlourishForeverStorage`. Someone migrating real user data should preserve backups and explicitly test how the older SavedVariables file becomes available.

A second detail is that **settings persist but cooldown history doesn't**. The last-emote timestamps exist only as a local Lua table in the runtime module, so reload and relog reset them. The program does not keep a ledger of emotes it has played or synchronize cooldowns among characters or other addon users.

The full `/flourish status` output reports whether the system is enabled, the number of configured abilities, and a diagnostic profile identifier containing the character GUID. That can be useful for debugging, but the identifying status should be redacted in public screenshots.

## What the next chapter should actually observe

The next useful evidence will come from the Forever release client: select one ability, check an emote, and cast it repeatedly at known timestamps. Watch what happens at 0%, 100%, under a cooldown, after a reload, and when a cast succeeds but does not land damage. Try two configured abilities in quick succession and verify that one doesn't consume the other's cooldown. Switch characters and confirm saved choices stay separate.

Then inspect the creative quality: Does the random flourish make a character feel more alive, or does a particular combination become repetitive? Which gestures convey the right personality? Do two fast emotes overwhelm normal social play? These are design findings for me to make in the game itself, not things an assistant can certify from source alone.

Flourish Forever is a compact demonstration of **authored spontaneity**: the player chooses the moments and possible actions, and a modest system adds variation at playtime. The technical work matters because its restraints—per-character preferences, chance, cooldown, successful-cast events and honest data migration—let that spontaneous character expression remain under the player's control.

# Flourish Forever — technical architecture

**Target:** World of Warcraft Forever 1.60.1, interface 16001.  
**Latest confirmed Git tag:** `v0.4.3-beta` · **Unreleased work:** `feat/ability-trigger-modes`.  
**Evidence:** current Lua source, package configuration, mocked test suites and Babuni's November 5, 2026 general in-game confirmation.


## New chosen-emote ability lock (development implementation, 7 November)

`cfg.emotes[token].cooldown` is still the 0–120-second duration set by each slider. The runtime **does not independently filter tokens using old last-fire history**. At the next eligible trigger it tests `RemainingAbilityLock` for that configured ability, rolls chance, then randomly chooses a token (native-only for asynchronous Success/Failure outcomes). The selected token's duration is snapshotted into `cfg.abilityLock = { token, duration, startedAt }` and `activeAbilityLocks[key]`. Until that duration expires, no other emote can trigger for that ability, regardless of its own configured duration. Locks for other ability keys are entirely separate.

The local `GetTime()` copy provides precision without polling; the persisted `GetServerTime()` timestamp survives `/reload`. Invalid saved locks are discarded. Slider changes affect the **next** lock only. A duration of zero imposes no lock apart from the existing short duplicate-action-hook suppression. `/flourish cooldowns [ability]` reports the chosen token and its active lock as well as each selected emote's *potential* lock duration.

Native `C_ChatInfo.PerformEmote(token)` is never called when actual chat lockdown prevents it. If invoked, the selected duration starts the ability lock whether the native API reports true or false, while the separate `lastFiredAt` and `lastAttemptAt` token stamps remain truthful historical evidence. A successfully submitted custom `/e` also starts the chosen duration, but outcome-triggered custom chat remains prohibited. Chance failure and empty/invalid pools impose no new lock. The prior per-token independent readiness model is retained in dated project history, not in current dispatch logic.

**Evidence:** GitHub mocked Lua tests and upload-disabled preview ZIP validation passed; Babuni's earlier individual timers worked in-game, but this revised ability-wide behavior has no reported live verification yet.

## Native retry attempt tracking (development; client verification pending)

The runtime now distinguishes three concepts: the **user's configured per-emote cooldown**, a native **API call attempt**, and an API-acknowledged **successful emote dispatch**. `cfg.emotes[token].lastFiredAt` records only successful native API returns (and custom `/e` dispatches), while `lastAttemptAt` records actual native `C_ChatInfo.PerformEmote(token)` invocations even if the function returns false. The latter is a bounded retry interval rather than evidence that the emote appeared. Both are Unix seconds; `lastFireByAbility[key][token]` holds the precise in-session last call time.

`RemainingCooldown` takes the longest active interval from the session clock, accepted-dispatch stamp and native-attempt stamp. `ReadyEmotes` shares this calculation with `/flourish cooldowns`; the report shows separate `savedStamp` and `attemptStamp`. A rejected native call updates only `lastAttemptAt`, never the accepted counter or `lastFiredAt`. Chance rejection, suppression due to actual chat lockdown and an unavailable API do not start the retry. If configured for zero seconds, both intervals are disabled, leaving only short duplicate-hook suppression.

The motivation is Babuni's actual Forever test: all nine native attempts reported false, but emotes appeared on repeated presses. Whether a false-result `PerformEmote` itself produces a local animation or another addon is responsible is still unknown. Applying the token's configured retry delay prevents repeated API calls without claiming successful emotes; it may also delay retries after genuine failures. The false-result-visible regression is a mock of that observation, **not in-game proof**.

## Per-token cooldown live diagnostics (unreleased)

The timer now has a single `RemainingCooldown(info, now, last, wallNow)` helper, returning the maximum nonexpired local (`GetTime()`) and saved server-time (`GetServerTime()`) remaining delay. Both `ReadyEmotes` and the manual `FlourishForever_CooldownDiagnostics(abilityName)` function call this helper. This refactor changes **no intended user-visible cooldown semantics**; it prevents the live report and selection code from disagreeing on timer calculations.

`/flourish cooldowns [ability name]` is read-only: it examines the active profile's selected tokens (up to twelve), each selected timer, session and saved last-dispatch stamp, and the last attempted token/dispatch result. If no name is supplied, it uses the last configured ability reached by a spell hook. `/flourish debug` adds the last ability, selected token, and configured per-token cooldown to its existing counters. These functions are invoked only manually, do not call a protected API, and do not mutate SavedVariables.

A player press dispatches at most one randomly chosen **ready token**; a six-second cooldown applies to that one token, not to the configured ability. Several selected tokens with separate cooldowns can therefore generate an emote on each of several successive presses without any token violating its own timer. The observed real-client repeating emote might follow that pattern or reflect a separate bug; it is **not diagnosed** without token-level evidence. Regression tests cover both patterns on the same version. No game-client verification is claimed.

## Per-emote cooldown persistence (development only)

Each selected emote uses `cfg.emotes[token].cooldown` (0–120 seconds) and may include `cfg.emotes[token].lastFiredAt` (integer Unix seconds from `GetServerTime()`). Both values live inside the character's existing SavedVariables profile and are keyed by configured ability and native/custom emote token. In-session `lastFireByAbility[key][token]` still uses high-resolution `GetTime()`, while `ReadyEmotes` requires both the in-session and persisted wall-clock checks to expire before selecting a token. This retains sub-second precision between reloads and prevents the previous reload bypass.

Only `RememberEmote` writes the wall timestamp when a native `C_ChatInfo.PerformEmote` reports success or the custom `/e` dispatch returns success. Chance rejection or no eligible token do not update the timer. The subsequent development correction records `lastAttemptAt` for native API false returns, imposing a retry interval without changing `lastFiredAt`. A zero-second preference is never blocked by its timestamp. Increasing/decreasing a slider applies to the elapsed time since the last dispatch. `NormalizeEmotes` discards impossible saved stamps, including NaN, infinity and non-positive values. Future clock values do not create an indefinite lock.

`GetServerTime()` is available on the Forever 1.60.1 API and gives Unix seconds, with one-second precision for persisted durations; `GetTime()` tracks the exact per-session elapsed interval. There is no `OnUpdate`, scheduled callback, timer scanning or addon communication. A UI reload recreates the precise Lua table but leaves each saved last-dispatch time intact.

**Evidence:** automatic Lua mocks test individual tokens, 0/15/30/60/120-second boundaries, independent abilities, a simulated fresh module load, and corrupt saves. The actual in-game report prompted the fix, but no post-fix in-client timer test is recorded.

## Search and PvP observability (development only)

Search rows store the displayed slash-command label for the UI, but their case-insensitive search index now concatenates the underlying native token with that label. This permits finding `ROAR` even if an alias or localization makes the displayed command different. The saved token remains unchanged.

For `press`, `TryAbilityEmoteFromPress` no longer rejects attempts when `C_Spell.IsSpellUsable` (or its legacy equivalent) reports false. Usability is not a security permission, and the trigger is the player's action attempt rather than spell execution. The existing 0.2-second duplicate-press limit and per-token cooldown remain active.

Session-only `debugState` tracks player-action hook calls, spell-outcome events, attempted emotes, reported API successes/refusals, last numeric spellID and a short reason. `FlourishForever_EmoteDiagnostics()` reads `IsInInstance()`, `InChatMessagingLockdown()`, and `GetAddOnRestrictionState` for `Chat`/`PvPMatch`, returning a concise status line for `/flourish debug`. No background polling, SavedVariables writes, player identifiers or automated output. A native API success boolean confirms only that the call was accepted, not that nearby players saw the emote.

The new diagnostic tool is intended to distinguish an unobserved player-action hook from a game security denial. The presence of a PvP restriction **does not by itself** establish chat lockdown; the two states must be observed separately. Client enforcement of `C_ChatInfo.PerformEmote()` in battlegrounds is unverified.

## Trigger-mode engine (development only)

`FlourishForever_ActionEmotes.lua` now validates `cfg.trigger` as `success` (default), `press`, or `failure` for each saved ability. The editor dropdown next to Chance updates only that ability's setting. No default is written to a different character's profile.

```text
Player action hook:
  configured mode=press -> native or custom emote immediately
  mode=success + battleground/arena -> temporary press fallback (if chat allowed)
  other modes -> no emote on press

Player UNIT_SPELLCAST_SUCCEEDED:
  mode=success + no PvP/chat restriction -> native eligible token only

Player UNIT_SPELLCAST_FAILED / FAILED_QUIET / INTERRUPTED:
  mode=failure + no PvP/chat restriction -> native eligible token only

No outcome callback may send custom /e chat (Forever requires hardware input).
Both paths retain per-ability chance and individual token cooldown.
```

PvP fallback is derived from `IsInInstance()` (`pvp`/`arena`) every time; it does not persist. Player-action dispatch checks actual `InChatMessagingLockdown()` and `Chat` restrictions; asynchronous outcomes additionally suppress PvP matches. `Map`/`Encounter`/`ChallengeMode` addon data restrictions do not block party/dungeon/raid expression. Restricted native APIs can still fail; this branch has no live game-client compatibility proof yet.

Outcome reports are deduplicated by non-secret cast GUID when available, falling back to a short same-spell/event window. Failure includes interruptions and quiet failures. Not every invalid button attempt creates a cast-failure event. Successful cast is not a confirmed hit.

The popup dropdown is a lightweight local frame with three choices, not a new dependency. It is contained inside the existing four-page UI; SaveVariables and runtime package layout remain unchanged.
## Runtime files and load order

```text
FlourishForever.toc
  ## Interface: 16001
  ## SavedVariables: FlourishForeverStorage
  1. FlourishForever_Storage.lua       -> per-GUID persistent profile
  2. FlourishForever.lua               -> slash command dispatch
  3. FlourishForever_ActionEmotes.lua  -> spellbook, emote engine, UI, hooks
```

There is no external library or server component.

## Profile model and migration

The account-wide `FlourishForeverStorage.profiles[UnitGUID("player")]` contains `actionEmotesEnabled`, an `instances` table keyed by normalized spell name, and `customEmotes` with text and stable `id` values. An ability entry holds `name`, `spellID`, `enabled`, `chance`, legacy/default `cooldown`, and `emotes` mapping selected native tokens or `c:id` custom tokens to `{ cooldown = seconds, lastFiredAt = optionalServerUnixSeconds }` on the current development branch.

`FlourishForever_BindCharacterDB` binds a character profile at login and from other DB entry points. It can migrate older name or name-realm keys into the current GUID key, and conditionally adopt an already-loaded `ROARitFOREVERStorage` global. It cannot load another addon's absent SavedVariables file.

`EnsureDB` bounds chance and cooldowns, handles malformed master/ability switches, preserves otherwise unrecognized records for manual recovery, and translates previous `ROAR = true` and other boolean emotes to per-token cooldown tables using the saved ability cooldown. An intentionally empty emote pool remains silent. Valid token entries are normalized in place, not repeatedly copied; the custom-emote list itself is normalized on access.

## Spellbook and UI

Spellbook data is discovered using the Forever client's `C_SpellBook` family, with guarded legacy fallback where present. Passive, off-spec, future and non-spell entries are skipped; ID/name deduplication and sorting protect the list. The available-ability UI groups the spellbook into categorized columns; search filters the cached results.

`CreateUI` constructs an 810×676 movable window with four pages: configured-ability overview, spellbook picker, ability editor and custom-text editor. The overview and picker each have a search field; the ability editor has a third search for native/custom emotes, individual cooldown sliders, per-ability chance and enable/disable. The editor preserves custom IDs where possible when saving edited text. The actual UI has been used in-game by Babuni, but exhaustive UI/combat states are not proven.

## Group-play guard refinement — 0.4.3-beta candidate

The `0.4.2-beta` player-action handler incorrectly treated `Map`, `Encounter` and `ChallengeMode` restriction states as reasons to skip every emote. These states signal restrictions on addon information and features, not necessarily a restriction on the player-triggered chat APIs. When active during group/instance play, this policy could suppress Flourish without a chat failure.

In the 0.4.3-beta candidate, `IsRestrictedEmoteContext()` instead checks only explicitly relevant conditions: `IsInInstance()` reporting `pvp` or `arena`, `C_ChatInfo.InChatMessagingLockdown()`, and `GetAddOnRestrictionState` for `Chat` and `PvPMatch` (including `Activating`). Normal party/raid membership and `Map`/`Encounter`/`ChallengeMode` data restrictions are not automatic reasons to suppress a player-action emote. Native and custom emotes share this check. No deferred chat retries or protected-function bypasses exist.

These conditions preserve security checks but cannot prove the client allows a particular emote. The new group behavior has mocked coverage, and Babuni reported the development version seems to work fine in-game. Specific dungeon, raid and protected-action scenarios remain unverified.

## Protected emote restrictions — 0.4.2-beta candidate

The public `v0.4.1-beta` tag still calls deprecated `DoEmote` from `UNIT_SPELLCAST_SUCCEEDED`. A subsequent BugGrabber report caught the same protected `PerformEmote()` call, demonstrating that checking only `IsInInstance()` for `pvp` and `arena` is insufficient.

The release candidate never registers `UNIT_SPELLCAST_SUCCEEDED` or calls the native emote API from an asynchronous event. Native and custom emotes share direct player `UseAction`, `CastSpellByID` and `C_Spell.CastSpell` hooks where supported.

```text
Player ability press -> identify action spell -> resolve configured ability
  -> IsInInstance: suppress pvp/arena
  -> C_ChatInfo.InChatMessagingLockdown: suppress during chat security state
  -> C_RestrictedActions.GetAddOnRestrictionState:
       suppress Chat/PvPMatch when activating or active;
       unrelated Map/Encounter/ChallengeMode restrictions do not block
  -> check ability enabled, emote pool, per-emote cooldown, and chance
  -> custom c:id: send EMOTE chat message in the press context
  -> native token: C_ChatInfo.PerformEmote(token) in the press context
  -> consume token cooldown only when the native API reports success

SPELLS_CHANGED -> refresh spellbook picker data when applicable
UNIT_SPELLCAST_SUCCEEDED -> not registered, never dispatches an emote
```

**Behavioral limitation:** an action press may not complete a successful spellcast, yet the experimental implementation may already have played an emote. A cast through a path not intercepted by the configured hooks may not trigger a flourish. Babuni reported no noticeable difference in ordinary gameplay and requested release; this timing change and its limitations are documented explicitly.

The modern `C_ChatInfo.PerformEmote` API is documented for Forever 1.60.1 with restrictions, but whether it actually succeeds in all relevant hardware-press/combat contexts remains **unverified in-game**. The guards are preventative, not circumventions. They cannot guarantee that all `ADDON_ACTION_BLOCKED` situations disappear. No deferred retries, synthetic clicks or protected API bypasses were added.

Cooldown timers are per ability and emote token. The current development build retains last-fired timestamps both in session memory for precision and in per-emote SavedVariables for reload persistence. Native API refusal does not count as a successful emote, but actual rejected calls now consume the separate per-token retry interval in development. The expanded interface and other character settings are otherwise unchanged.

## Source-level tradeoffs

**Cast success versus damage hit:** The original introductory text said “when that ability lands.” The actual implementation observes **UNIT_SPELLCAST_SUCCEEDED**. That avoids parsing combat damage/target effects but may emit a flourish even when a cast later misses, is resisted or has no meaningful target hit. No new trigger is approved.

**Name-key versus ID-key:** The event carries a spell ID and the UI lists spellbook IDs, but saved configurations are keyed by **normalized spell name**. This can make multiple ranks share one expressive identity, while risking same-name collisions and localization-induced mismatches.

**Independent cooldowns versus global social volume (original model):** The 0.3.x version gave every configured ability its own timestamp; there is no overall emote budget. That respects distinctive spell personalities but two different abilities can emote close together. Any future global throttling is a creator decision.

**Cooldown only on a fired emote:** A failed chance check or empty emote pool doesn't consume it. Chance therefore determines frequency independently from the *last actual emote*, though the zero default timestamp may suppress a very early first attempt.

**Transient runtime state versus persisted preferences:** Ability choices persist by GUID; timers reset on UI reload/relog. This is simpler but won't provide a durable anti-spam cooldown if a player logs in and out quickly.

**Native emotes versus custom writing (revised in 0.4.0-beta):** The original scope was native token discovery only. The expanded version also supports player-written `/e` lines; they still do not create new sounds or animations, and must be triggered during a player-button press.

**Legacy compatibility versus fully automatic migration:** Current source can adopt `ROARitFOREVERStorage` only when already loaded. It doesn't read an arbitrary old disk file. Name-realm legacy keys are not evidence of separate game realms on Forever.

**Packaging vs release assets:** The repository has CurseForge packager metadata and two GitHub release entries with no attached assets. No installer, ZIP checksum or distribution success should be invented.

## Unapproved questions for later discussion

Should cooldowns survive reload? Should live hits (when knowable) be used rather than cast success? Should duplicated spell names be distinct configurations? Should a global emote frequency ceiling coexist with per-ability cooldowns? Should there be a preview button? The repository now mirrors its pre-existing CurseForge MIT license; no new public release has been approved. Record Babuni's choice before treating any other alternative as accepted.

# Flourish Forever — emote content, character settings and assets

**Creative direction:** Babuni · **Portfolio:** babuni.dev · **Target:** World of Warcraft Forever / interface 16001.  
**Public baseline:** v0.4.3-beta · **Development:** Success/press/failure choice per ability, pending in-game verification.


## Chosen emote determines the active ability lock (development)

The cooldown slider still writes `cfg.emotes[token].cooldown` (0–120 seconds) for each selected emote. New ability-level state is `cfg.abilityLock = { token = "ROAR", duration = 20, startedAt = unixSeconds }`, persisted in the same GUID-keyed character profile. This record represents the **last selected emote's ability-wide cooldown**, not a fixed configured ability timer. A three-second token locks its own ability for three seconds; a twenty-second token locks it for twenty, excluding every other selected token during that interval.

Legacy per-token `lastFiredAt` and `lastAttemptAt` values remain available for historical diagnostics and truthful API-result reporting, but do not gate which token may be selected. Separate abilities and character profiles retain independent locks; no global character cooldown was introduced.

## Content sources

| Content | Source | Persistence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spell names, IDs, icons and categories | Player spellbook and spell APIs | Name/key/ID in configured abilities |
| Native emotes | Client `EMOTE*_TOKEN` globals, with ROAR fallback | Token-keyed selection and cooldown |
| Custom `/e` text | Player-authored text entered in the custom emote editor | `customEmotes` entries with stable IDs |
| Per-ability chance and enabled switch | Player configuration | Character profile |
| Per-emote cooldowns | Player configuration | Emote selection records |
| Last successful dispatch / native retry attempt (development) | Session `GetTime()` plus `lastFiredAt` and `lastAttemptAt` from `GetServerTime()` | Separate per-character/per-emote timestamps; both delay types survive reload/relog |

## Per-ability trigger preference (development)

Each configured ability may include `trigger = "success"`, `"press"`, or `"failure"`. Older and malformed records normalize to `"success"` without deleting saved emote preferences. The value is per ability and per character, rather than global. Battleground/arena fallback is computed at runtime and is never saved.

Native tokens can be considered on success/failure events, but custom `c:id` /e text is only sent during a genuine hardware press. As a result, selecting only custom emotes with Success or Failure yields no automatic message in those contexts. The ability editor communicates this limitation; it is not evidence of a broken SavedVariables migration.
## Storage and defaults

The TOC declares `SavedVariables: FlourishForeverStorage`. Profiles are isolated by `UnitGUID("player")`, and configured abilities are keyed by normalized spell name. The base data shape is:

```lua
FlourishForeverStorage = {
  profiles = {
    ["<player GUID>"] = {
      actionEmotesEnabled = true,
      customEmotes = { { id = "1", text = "waves a tiny flag." } },
      instances = {
        ["<normalized spell name>"] = {
          name = "Spell Name",
          spellID = 123,
          enabled = true,
          chance = 100,
          cooldown = 6, -- retained migration/default value
          emotes = {
            ROAR = { cooldown = 6 },
            ["c:1"] = { cooldown = 12 },
          }
        },
      },
    },
  },
}
```

This is a structural illustration, not an actual character profile. A new character has no configured abilities. The first added ability starts with native ROAR selected; user-defined emotes are never assigned without explicit player choice.

Older `cfg.emotes[token] = true` entries are normalized into `{ cooldown = legacyAbilityCooldown }`; valid per-emote tables are retained. Unsupported SavedVariables records remain recoverable where possible. Stored cooldown preferences persist. On the development branch, `lastFiredAt` stores the last accepted native/custom dispatch and `lastAttemptAt` stores the last actual native API call even if its return was false. Both are per token; precise in-session timing remains separate. A false result never establishes successful output.

Custom emotes have `c:`-prefixed saved references and text entries under `customEmotes`. Deleting or editing custom lines can affect assigned selections; the editor tries to preserve IDs where corresponding lines remain.

- `/flourish`, `/flourishforever`, `/rit`, `/ffsh` open the UI; `/flourish status` gives the current diagnostic summary.

# Gather Map

**A self-learning resource map overlay for World of Warcraft 1.12**

**Creator:** Babuni.dev  
**Addon version:** 0.4.3 · **Interface:** 11200 · **SavedVariables:** `GatherMapDB`  
**Implementation:** [`GatherMap.lua`](GatherMap.lua), [`GatherMap.toc`](GatherMap.toc)  
**Documentation audit:** 2026-10-26 — verified against source and Git history; **no new in-game tests performed**.

Gather Map remembers **where you successfully gathered resources** and shows those discoveries on both the minimap and zone world map. It started as a herbalism tool and grew into a broader record of herbs, minerals, custom Survival trees, skinned loot, lockpicking chests and ordinary treasure chests. The map learns as you play: **it does not import an authoritative catalog of currently available spawns**.

Instead of opaque dots, the overlay uses **four small difficulty-colored corner markers**. The world map also shows the associated resource icon. Markers re-evaluate against the *current character's* skill or level, while discoveries remain available across the account.

![Saved herbs on the Tanaris world map](Screenshots/world-map-tanaris.png)

## What is recorded

| Resource kind | How it is learned | How color is determined | When it is visible |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Herbs** | Gather completion or recognized loot after Interact | Herbalism requirement | Current character has Herbalism |
| **Minerals** | Mining success, with some loot-to-node fallback | Mining requirement | Current character has Mining |
| **Survival trees** | Successful Woodcutting/recognized tree loot | Survival requirement | Current character has Survival |
| **Skinning** | Looted hide/leather/scale/item after skinning; saved as an approximate hunting spot | Requirement inferred from creature level | Current character has Skinning |
| **Lockpicking chests** | Recognized locked chest interaction | Lockpicking requirement | Current character has Lockpicking |
| **Ordinary chests** | Recognized world chest interaction | Known chest tier compared with character level | All characters |

The code associates a resource with a zone, subzone, map position, type, requirement where known, icon where available, and occurrence count. The main database is **account-wide**, but profession filtering and colors adapt to each character. **Skinning markers indicate places where a creature was skinned, not guaranteed stationary spawns.**

Custom resource tooltips can supply requirements; unknown requirements produce **purple** corners instead of an invented difficulty. A few known loot-to-node mappings are deliberately cautious: Thorium Ore alone cannot reveal a small versus rich Thorium vein.

## Two map presentations


### Minimap — subtle four-corner markers

Saved locations currently in range appear as four colored corners, with a hover label. The minimap visualization uses coordinates, zoom state, estimated scaling and custom-zone dimensions to position markers.

![Minimap marker and tooltip](Screenshots/minimap-tooltip.png)

### World map — resource icons plus corners

When you open a specific **zone** on the world map, saved locations appear with their matching resource icon and corner dots. The **Gather Map** checkbox near the upper-left of the map toggles this overlay separately from the minimap. It remembers that setting.

![Merged resource markers](Screenshots/world-map-merged-markers.png)

Nearby markers for the **same resource kind and name** merge if their marker bounds overlap. Their four corner dots expand to the outside of the combined rectangle. Different resources do **not** merge. The rendering code caps each map at **300 displayed marker groups**; this is a display cap, **not a cap on saved discoveries**.

### Difficulty colors

| Color | Profession requirement compared with current skill |
| --- | --- |
| Red | Skill below the requirement |
| Orange | Skill meets the requirement, up to 24 points above |
| Yellow | 25–49 above |
| Green | 50–99 above |
| Gray | 100+ above |
| Purple | Requirement unknown |

For ordinary treasure, the algorithm compares the **chest tier to player level**, not profession skill: red at 6+ levels above; orange 3–5 above; yellow from 2 below through 2 above; green 3–9 below; gray 10+ below; unknown purple. Gray has **85% opacity**, the other categories 100%.

## Commands

| Command | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `/gathermap`, `/gathermap count`, `/gathermap status` | Show saved counts by type, profession skills and current zone support |
| `/gmap` | Alias for the same slash command family |
| `/gathermap on` or `show` | Show **minimap** markers |
| `/gathermap off` or `hide` | Hide **minimap** markers but continue recording discoveries |
| World-map **Gather Map** checkbox | Independently show/hide the **world-map** overlay |

The two visibility choices live in `GatherMapDB.enabled` and `GatherMapDB.worldMapEnabled`. Turning off minimap pins does **not** stop gathering or necessarily hide world-map pins.

## Install

1. Copy the project folder to `World of Warcraft/Interface/AddOns/GatherMap/`. Place `GatherMap.lua`, `GatherMap.toc` and `Icons/` inside that folder together.
2. Restart WoW, enable **Gather Map**, and use **Load out of date AddOns** if your particular 1.12-compatible client requires it.
3. Gather a recognized resource successfully, then run `/gmap count` and check the minimap/world map for the learned point.
4. Optionally install [Interact](https://github.com/lookino/Interact) for its hotkey behavior; Gather Map does **not require** it.

**Compatibility:** The TOC declares interface **11200**. The source includes additional outdoor/event map sizes for named custom zones; that is not proof every third-party 1.12 client has been verified. Several event strings, profession names, resource names and tooltip patterns are in English; **full localized-client support has not been demonstrated**.

## Supported custom maps

The current `customZoneSize` table contains **15** names: Hyjal, Scarlet Enclave, Lapidis Isle, Gillijim's Isle, Tel'Abim, Alah'Thalas, Gilneas, Icepoint Rock, Blackstone Island, Thalassian Highlands, Winter Veil Vale, Grim Reaches, Balor, Northwind and Moonwhisper Coast. The source has aliases including “Mount Hyjal” and “Island of Lapidis.” Subareas belonging to an existing Vanilla map may reuse their parent map's scaling.

A zone's presence in the table only establishes a **configured dimension**, not confirmed correct minimap alignment on every custom client.

![Markers in the custom Grim Reaches zone](Screenshots/world-map-grim-reaches.png)

## Upgrade if you used the old name

This project was originally named **Octo Gather**. Renaming the folder and saved-variable name does **not automatically migrate** old `OctoGatherDB` data into `GatherMapDB`.

With WoW **fully closed**, install `GatherMap` beside the old addon, open PowerShell in the new addon folder, and run the supplied migration helper with paths you supply:

```powershell
.\Upgrade-SavedData.ps1 -ClientPath "C:\Games\World of Warcraft" -PreviousAddonName "OctoGather"
```

The helper reads the old/new TOC declarations, scans saved-variable files, backs up sources in `AddonUpgradeBackups`, copies converted files to the new name, refuses existing destination files, and **does not execute saved Lua**. It leaves the original files in place. Disable the old addon, check the migrated data and retain the backups. The helper's contents were reviewed, but **it was not executed in this session**.

For non-Windows setups the older README includes a manual migration approach: back up your WTF SavedVariables first; copy old named SavedVariables files to the new name and change **only the top-level declaration** from the old TOC variable to `GatherMapDB`. Do not do this with WoW running.

For ordinary updates **without a folder/name change**, standard WoW SavedVariables persistence applies.

## How reliable is the data?

This is a **personal discovery record**, not a live-world sensing system. WoW's existing tracking dots may show a resource is currently spawned; Gather Map records places previously encountered. A failed cast should not create a node, but correctness depends on game event text, loot timing, tooltip availability and position APIs. The source contains debouncing and pending-state handling to reduce duplicates; these need client-level verification.

The current code polls map updates at approximately **0.10 seconds**, merges markers, and uses an upper display limit of 300 groups per map. Large saved databases, many custom zones, localized clients and interaction-hook load orders merit performance and compatibility tests.

The repo includes two regression-test scripts, **not an all-encompassing automated test suite**:
- `tests/test_interact_hook.py`: tests recursive Interact-hook behavior with **lupa / Lua 5.1** fixture code, not a live Vanilla client.
- `tests/test_upgrade.ps1`: tests migration from a synthetic previous addon name using temporary fixture directories.

Neither was executed during the 2026-10-26 documentation pass.

# GatherMap — concept and original creative direction

**Creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Public project:** Gather Map, formerly Octo Gather  
**Target:** Vanilla WoW 1.12-compatible addons, with additional named custom maps.

## Learn the world by exploring it

Rather than filling the map with an imported atlas from the start, Gather Map learns **from what the player actually gathers**. A successful action creates a local discovery that the player can recognize on a subsequent journey. It turns ordinary gathering into a gradual act of mapping.

That makes two forms of knowledge coexist: the world may contain a resource *now*, and the player may remember *where one previously appeared*. The addon deals in the second kind of knowledge. It does not know whether a mining vein or herb currently exists at a stored position. Skinning locations are even looser: they are memories of moving creatures yielding items, not static spawn-point promises.

The basic experience is personal and unobtrusive. It rewards curiosity and revisiting familiar routes without taking over navigation or gathering actions.

## A visible language of four corners

The visual system is intentionally different from a map full of solid opaque pins. **Four small corner dots** surround a location on the minimap; the world map adds the recognizable resource artwork inside those corners. The corner colors describe how hard the resource would be for the **character currently playing**. Red is too difficult, orange is just reachable, yellow and green become easier, gray is old territory, and purple communicates uncertainty.

A single account-wide memory can therefore look different for an experienced herbalist and a character who has yet to learn the profession. The data belongs to the player; the presentation is contextual.

When same-resource markers overlap, the dots are pushed to the outside of the merged group instead of stacking a blur of duplicate frames. Distinct resource types remain independent.

## From herbs to a broader ecology

The first September 5 version documented herbs. The September 6 commits expanded the world that could be remembered: minerals, chests, skinning, woodcutting trees and profession-aware hiding. This growth is a meaningful creative turn—not merely a bigger database. Each resource asks a different question of the interface:
- A herb or ore deposit has a fixed node, often a known gathering requirement.
- A chest may have a skill lock or only a tier relative to the character's level.
- A skinned creature leaves behind a hunting memory, not a node.
- A custom Survival tree belongs to a profession absent from standard Vanilla 1.12.
- Unknown custom resources may reveal their own requirements through a tooltip, or remain honestly purple.

The current implementation accommodates those distinctions while keeping one consistent visual vocabulary.

## The engineering context is part of the work

Additional client maps do not necessarily preserve numeric zone indices from classic Gatherer. The implementation uses zone names, aliases and specific scaling dimensions; it also handles an optional Interact hotkey API. The September 7 fix for recursion after other addons wrap `Interact` demonstrates how an apparently simple quality-of-life project has to cope with shared, mutable game-client functions.

In September the project moved from **Octo Gather** to the more provider-neutral **Gather Map** identity. The rename was both technical and documentary because SavedVariables, icon paths and installation names had to match—and old saved data needed a careful migration.

## Creative authorship, not an invented origin story

These principles are grounded in the original README, feature history and current source. The available commits do **not** reproduce all of Babuni.dev's original thinking or show who drafted every function. The creator's core ideas and direction remain credited to Babuni.dev. The AI documentation assistant's later analysis and wording are a separate contribution.

Do not replace this living exploration record with a generic imported-mining database, excessive map clutter or a conventional web-map dashboard without the creator's decision.

# GatherMap — narrative development journal

**Original creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Retrospective written:** October 26, 2026 from GitHub commits, repository README, Lua, migration utility, tests and screenshots. No missing original chat transcript has been fabricated.

## The first idea: let the map learn the player's routes

Gather Map began as **Octo Gather**, a Vanilla 1.12 map addon that learned a location *after* the player successfully picked a herb. It wasn't meant to supply a permanent imported atlas that magically knew every resource spawn. The player discovers something, and the client remembers it for later.

That distinction is the heart of the creative contribution. It is modest in terms of interface but meaningful in terms of experience: the world becomes legible through play. The record is **account-wide**, yet the markers can change their colors when another character views the same place with a different profession skill.

The initial substantive commit, **`0cd8e97` on September 5, 2026**, arrived as “Initial Octo Gather release.” It included a nearly finished herbalism prototype, `OctoGather.lua`, a 1.12 TOC at version **0.2.6**, 29 herb art files, and four documentation screenshots. That first version displayed saved herbs on both the minimap and selected zone world map with difficulty-colored rectangular outlines. It read current Herbalism skill and compared it against requirements, initially drawing a maximum of 100 pins.

The source already credited [Gatherer](https://github.com/jsb/Gatherer) for original zone scaling and herb artwork and [MetaHunt](https://github.com/DuvelCorp/MetaHunt) for the Grim Reaches map dimensions. Those aren't incidental footnotes: using verified existing map geometry and recognizable game artwork made the creator's own recording and UI logic usable in an older game client. The portfolio must distinguish **Babuni.dev's creative/system design** from those upstream resources.

The original repository history does not contain a separate recorded ideation conversation. This journal interprets the intent through the README and code, rather than claiming to quote an unavailable design discussion.

## September 6: the herb notebook becomes a resource atlas

The next day's changes were unusually concentrated. Commit **`7d4d029`** expanded the program to learn **mining, skinning, locked chests and ordinary treasure**. The data format needed a `kind` field because one location could no longer mean only “herb.” The addon started handling more tooltip, cast, loot and skill information to make those categories recognizable; the maximum rendered group count increased to 300.

That expansion revealed that not all “resource locations” mean the same thing. An herb sits at a ground node. Mining loot may identify its likely ore source, though it may not uniquely identify a vein. A skinned hide is produced by a **moving creature**, so a saved point is a useful hunting memory rather than a reliable stationary node. Locked chests use **Lockpicking** difficulty, while ordinary chests lack profession requirements and instead use a tier relative to the player's level.

Two later September 6 commits show small, deliberate improvements to accuracy: **`4eabd57`** corrected the difficulty formula for low-level skinnable creatures, and **`bd98a2d`** mapped known skin materials to better inventory icons. The current internal DB migration later clears older unreliable skin requirements while keeping saved locations—evidence that the design values preserving player discoveries more than preserving every early formula result.

The same day, **`8f890b2`** hid nodes when the current character lacked their profession, without deleting them from account-wide storage. This change protected readability. A new character shouldn't be confronted with every previous herbalism memory unless it has a reason to use it.

Then **`bec4f92`** added **Survival Woodcutting** and six specific tree types: Simple, Bright, Shade, Tropical, Dead and Star Wood. This mattered because the custom-client ecosystem supported a profession that standard Vanilla didn't. The project was becoming a flexible place-memory system rather than a fixed table of old Blizzard herbs.

## September 7: a visual language becomes distinct

The project originally used full colored rectangular outlines. Commit **`dc6f4ba`**, “Replace marker outlines with corner dots,” transformed that into **four small colored corner dots** on the minimap and a resource icon nested within four dots on the world map.

The system continues to group overlapping markers for the **same resource** into one larger rectangle; but the rectangle is now expressed only by its outer corners, leaving the underlying native map more visible. When a line of same-resource marker bounds overlaps transitively, the merge algorithm repeatedly checks the growing group. Other resources are kept independent, preventing a confusing combined cluster that means no particular thing.

Later that day **`9572119`** increased gray marker opacity to **85%** and refreshed screenshots. That is a concrete usability iteration, not merely a CSS-style cosmetic tweak. A marker representing an easy or low-value node still needs to remain visible enough to be useful.

The user-facing map has two independent display toggles. One is the chat command controlling minimap markers; another is the world-map checkbox. Hiding pins doesn't erase previously learned data, which fits the project's original premise of accumulating exploration memory.

## September 7: learning to coexist with other addons

The commit **`1cb631f`**, “Prevent recursive Interact hook chains,” tackles a technical problem that is especially interesting in a portfolio narrative. Gather Map supports the optional [Interact](https://github.com/lookino/Interact) hotkey. It needs to notice when that API is used because a subsequent loot event may identify a resource even when the game never exposed an ordinary object tooltip.

But WoW addons can replace global Lua functions. If Gather Map's wrapper always consults **one shared variable** holding a previous `Interact` function, another addon can wrap Gather Map, which then rewraps that addon, causing the supposedly old function reference to point into the new chain. The result can be recursive calls rather than one clean delegation.

The revised `InstallInteractHook` closes over a **different predecessor for each installed wrapper**, so an older wrapper continues pointing to the function it was created to wrap. It also checks for repeated installs and is invoked during later update checks to notice replacement.

That fix came with **`tests/test_interact_hook.py`**, a narrow regression fixture that uses Lua 5.1 through Python lupa to demonstrate the old chain's recursion and validate the new approach under synthetic conditions. The test is part of the project history; this documentation pass **did not execute it** and it cannot replace an actual WoW 1.12 integration test.

This is an example of why development process deserves a place in the finished portfolio: the visible result remains four harmless map corners, but it relies on subtle cooperation between independently authored addons.

## September 18: the project finds a more general identity

The September 18 commit **`0a01737`**, “Use provider-neutral names and client compatibility descriptions,” renamed **Octo Gather** to **Gather Map** throughout the addon title, Lua script, TOC, SavedVariables identifier, icon path and README. The manifest became version **0.4.3**.

The user-facing identity was broader, but the rename came with a technical cost. A player's old discoveries were in files named for the previous addon and a top-level variable **`OctoGatherDB`**. Simply changing the folder and enabling the new code would not automatically restore that data.

So the repository added **`Upgrade-SavedData.ps1`**: a migration helper that reads the TOC variables, copies relevant saved files, preserves originals, creates backups, refuses to overwrite an existing destination and rewrites top-level variable assignments without evaluating saved Lua. It also added **`tests/test_upgrade.ps1`** with synthetic account/character SavedVariables, Unicode text, backup checks and overwrite/path-name refusal checks.

This is a distinct iteration beyond maps and gathering. The project needed to respect the player's accumulated personal history precisely because the idea was to remember exploration. A migration that silently lost nodes would defeat the original concept.

No execution log for the PowerShell fixture was inspected in this audit. The source is a safeguard design, not proof that a user's actual files were successfully migrated.

The next visible commits on **October 26** updated the TOC/README author attribution to **Babuni.dev** and added a first set of short documentation files and links. The current documentation review expands those into a technical architecture, interaction-design record, content/provenance inventory, roadmap, decisions register and this narrative journal.

What does the player experience on a crowded minimap with hundreds of saved locations? How does the marker system feel for a Skinner who is chasing moving creatures rather than revisiting static resource nodes? How should custom map aliases be tested across game clients? When should the system prefer an unknown purple marker over a guessed requirement? These are productive next questions, not approvals to replace the existing system.

# GatherMap — technical architecture

**Source audited:** `GatherMap.lua` (1,237 lines), `GatherMap.toc`, saved-data helper and tests, October 26, 2026. **Static code review, not client execution.**

## Lifecycle, events and state

```text
ADDON_LOADED (GatherMap / optional Interact)
    -> InitializeDatabase()
    -> InstallInteractHook()

PLAYER_ENTERING_WORLD
    -> InitializeDatabase(), UpdatePins(), UpdateWorldMapPins()

SPELLCAST_START / CHAT_MSG_SPELL_SELF_BUFF / SPELLCAST_STOP
    -> BeginResourceAction() / recorded successful resource text
    -> RecordNodeOnce() if valid
SPELLCAST_FAILED / SPELLCAST_INTERRUPTED
    -> ClearPending()
CHAT_MSG_LOOT
    -> classify item and capture mining/herb/wood or skinning loot
SKILL_LINES_CHANGED / MINIMAP_UPDATE_ZOOM / ZONE_CHANGED_NEW_AREA
    -> refresh minimap and world-map markers
WORLD_MAP_UPDATE
    -> refresh world-map markers

OnUpdate approximately every 0.10 seconds
    -> expire pending loot
    -> InstallInteractHook() if global changed
    -> refresh pins, world pins and hovered labels
```

The source uses Vanilla 1.12's implicit `event`, `arg1`, `this` callback conventions and Lua 5.0 compatible syntax. The TOC loads one Lua file, optional-depends on `Interact`, and initializes account-wide `GatherMapDB`.

## Categories and gathering state machine

The current `actionKinds` table maps:
- `Herb Gathering` → herb
- `Mining` → mineral
- `Skinning` → skin
- `Woodcutting` → wood
- `Opening` → treasure
- `Pick Lock` → lock

`BeginResourceAction` reads the object tooltip or target context, storing **pendingNode**, **pendingRequirement**, **pendingKind**, **pendingTexture**, pending flag, and a time window for loot arriving after an interaction. A successful self-buff/action phrase such as `You perform ... on ...` may directly name a resource; `SPELLCAST_STOP` can commit a pending node if identified. Failures clear state. Skinning awaits loot so the record can name the **actual item** received.

`InstallInteractHook` watches the optional global `Interact`, records a last-interact timestamp, and delegates to the function that existed when the wrapper was created. On later replacement it can wrap again with a **new locally captured predecessor**; a shared predecessor previously produced recursive chains. The dedicated Python/Lua fixture tries to reproduce the old recursion and exercise the current wrapper. Interact itself is not bundled.

The **Interact loot fallback** can infer herbs, ore deposits or wood through recognized looted item names. Some names are inherently ambiguous (e.g. Thorium Ore can come from different vein types), so the source uses a generic node/unknown requirement instead of falsely choosing a specific deposit.

**Locale caution:** Several action names, English chat patterns, profession strings, chest keywords and resource names are literal English. This limits assertions of universal localization support.

## Data model and deduplication

```text
GatherMapDB
├── version = 3
├── enabled = true/false         # minimap overlay only
├── worldMapEnabled = true/false # independent world map
└── nodes
    └── "<continent>:<zone>" = [
          {
            name, kind, x, y, required?,
            texture?, count, zoneName, areaName
          }, ...
       ]
```

A resource's position is read from the player's current zone map, stored as normalized map coordinates. `RecordNode` rejects absent names/positions, finds same-type+name nodes within **0.004** in both X and Y, then updates their **weighted average position and count**. Otherwise it appends a new entry. `RecordNodeOnce` also suppresses same-kind+name events within **2 seconds**. These two mechanisms differ: the first groups repeated visits spatially, the second filters repeated event emissions temporally.

The key `"<continent>:<zone>"` uses the map indices in the **currently loaded client**. Added custom maps can change indices and zone mapping; migrating SavedVariables across clients with different zone indices needs special testing. `zoneName` and `areaName` are saved alongside positions, but the current primary lookup is still the numeric key.

On init, **old database version 1** entries missing `kind` become `herb`; old **version 2** skin points retain their location but have stale `required` cleared due to earlier low-level formula error. The current version is **3**.

## Current-skill presentation

The source reads skill lines named Herbalism, Mining, Skinning, Lockpicking and Survival. `ShouldShowNode` hides profession-based markers if the current character lacks the respective skill (rank 0); treasure always shows.

Profession colors compare requirement to current rank:
- unknown → purple;
- skill below required → red;
- skill required to required+24 → orange;
- +25..+49 → yellow;
- +50..+99 → green;
- +100 and above → gray.

Treasure uses player level instead of profession: required tier minus player level ≥6 red, ≥3 orange, ≥-2 yellow, ≥-9 green, otherwise gray.

Skinning requirement inversely calculates Vanilla's level/skill rule: creature level up to 10 yields 1; levels 11–20 use `(level - 10)*10`; above 20 use `level*5`. Saved skinning points name the **looted item**, not necessarily the creature name.

## Coordinate conversion and custom maps

`GetPosition` finds the current main map zone by normalized **zone name** (`GetRealZoneText` checked against `GetMapZones`), then uses `GetPlayerMapPosition`. It may call `SetMapZoom` to resolve (0,0) position when map not visible.

`zoneScale` maps normal zone names to classic Gatherer-derived factors; `continentScale` and `minimapZoomYards` convert zoom into minimap offsets. **15** `customZoneSize` width/height pairs enable extra event/custom maps. `zoneAliases` handles spelling variants such as Mount Hyjal → Hyjal. A custom map's configured dimensions are **not automatically a live-tested compatibility guarantee**.

## Rendering and interaction

- `UpdatePins` computes minimap offsets relative to player, applies visibility and a circular minimap radius. The minimap shows **four 3px colored corner dots** per grouped hit area, with hover labels.
- `UpdateWorldMapPins` requires an open specifically selected zone, not a continent overview. It converts normalized X/Y to the `WorldMapButton` dimensions, adds game/bundled resource icon textures and four corner dots.
- `AddMarkerGroup` merges overlapping rectangles **only for identical kind + name**, and rechecks after expansion for transitive overlap. The **highest difficulty priority** wins within a merged group; different resources can overlap without merging.
- A reusable pool of frames cuts repeated creation, and `MAX_PINS=300` limits groups **rendered** on each map, not database size.
- A separate custom cursor tooltip avoids dependence on fragile old tooltip templates while the game tooltip is used for gathering recognition.
- `GatherMapDB.enabled` controls minimap only; the world-map checkbox saves `worldMapEnabled` independently. Recording continues when markers are hidden.
- Gray groups have 85% alpha; other groups full alpha. The refresh loop triggers around **10 times per second**, which may be expensive on dense maps.

## Dependencies and migration helper

`GatherMap.toc` declares `OptionalDeps: Interact`; `Interact` is not required. Bundled `Icons/Herb*.tga` (29 files) are credited to [Gatherer](https://github.com/jsb/Gatherer) alongside minimap scaling. Grim Reaches map data is credited to [MetaHunt](https://github.com/DuvelCorp/MetaHunt).

`Upgrade-SavedData.ps1` supports renaming SavedVariables after the transition from **OctoGatherDB** to **GatherMapDB**. It checks that WoW is closed, limits addon-name input, reads old/new TOCs, backs up discovered SavedVariables, refuses overwrites and rewrites only top-level assignments in the copied text without executing Lua. This is separate from in-addon schema migration.

Two fixture tests are committed. `tests/test_interact_hook.py` requires **lupa/Lua 5.1**; `tests/test_upgrade.ps1` runs on PowerShell. Neither is evidence of client correctness absent execution logs.

**No actual game testing or helper execution occurred in this documentation-only review.**

# GatherMap — visual, navigation and interaction design

**Creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev.

## A map that remembers, not a map that reveals everything

Gather Map begins with a subtle design decision: it learns **after discovery**. The overlay is a personal memory of gathering and exploring, so it should remain recognizable as an annotation layer on the game's own maps rather than pretending to know live spawns.

The work is not an alternative full-screen navigation app. It attaches to the native **minimap** and **world map**, retaining their familiar spatial context.

## Four corners, space in the middle

A small resource is marked by **four 3-pixel colored corner dots**, leaving its center mostly clear on the minimap. When the world map is open, a resource icon sits inside matching colored corners. The design moved here from early full rectangular outlines, with a visible September 7 commit documenting that choice.

Hovering uses a separate compact label frame so the map can display the resource name without competing with the native GameTooltip used during gathering. This is especially appropriate in a 1.12 UI, where tooltip behavior and mouse layers vary.

![Minimap tooltip](../Screenshots/minimap-tooltip.png)

## Dynamic difficulty as a personal reading of the world

Red, orange, yellow, green, gray and purple are not static property labels printed on resources. They are interpretations relative to the **current character's skill or level**. Something once red can become gray as the player grows; an old account-wide discovery can become red again for a new character.

Purple is meaningful uncertainty: the addon cannot derive a requirement from its known table or an object tooltip. It avoids guessing. Gray uses **85% opacity**, a September adjustment from less legible variants.

Profession resources are hidden if the character doesn't know the corresponding skill. That keeps a low-level/new-profession minimap from becoming an irrelevant collection of everything the account has ever found. Ordinary treasure is the exception and can remain visible to any class.

## Grouping without erasing identity

Same-type and same-name markers merge when their drawn rectangles overlap. The group's four corners expand to the new overall bounds. If multiple nearby nodes have different requirements, the group's strongest difficulty priority is used. Resources with different names/types remain separate even when they overlap.

This prevents the visual clutter of duplicate marks without collapsing distinct types into meaningless giant boxes.

![Grouped world map markers](../Screenshots/world-map-merged-markers.png)

## Controls and affordances

The minimap overlay is governed by `/gmap on` / `off`, while a **Gather Map** checkbox on the world map controls the world overlay. Both are stored. No control removes learned locations or turns off discovery merely to hide markers.

The status command prints total saved points, type counts, skill ranks and whether the current zone has known scaling. This makes the system slightly diagnosable without introducing another settings window.

## Areas requiring genuine user testing

- Dense nodes vs. 300-group drawing cap.
- Different minimap sizes, UI scaling and indoor/outdoor zoom.
- Readability of colored 3px corner dots and 85%-opacity gray in varying environments.
- Hover zones and mouse-layer conflicts with other minimap addons.
- Whether skinning hunting areas need their own visual distinction from stationary herbs and ore.
- Whether hidden-profession defaults match the creator's preferred exploration style.

These are evaluation questions, **not** an approved redesign or a claimed accessibility test.

## Architectural tradeoffs visible today

- **Learned, not imported:** gives a personal exploration record; cannot show unknown locations or current live spawns.
- **Account-wide storage, character-aware rendering:** preserves one discovery memory but hides professions a given character cannot use.
- **Icon/resource-type categorization:** distinguishes herb, mining, wood, skin, locks and treasure, with each using a different requirement model.
- **Near-position deduplication:** uses a **0.004 x/y** window and weighted averaging, potentially combining distinct nodes located extremely close together.
- **Marker group merging:** combines the on-screen outlines for matching kind/name only, while leaving underlying saved database nodes untouched.
- **Ten redraws per second:** responsive to movement/zoom but potentially expensive for large saved databases.
- **Client zone indices:** compatibility with extra maps uses name lookup and custom sizes, but the primary DB key is still numeric continent/zone, which may shift across different clients.
- **English skill/action/tooltip matching:** avoids some complexity, but isn't guaranteed locale-neutral.
- **Optional Interact wrapping:** convenience requires careful wrapper chain ownership and regression coverage.
- **Rename with migration:** provider-neutral identity improves clarity but requires work to preserve earlier player data.
