# Group Buff Toggle

**Creator:** Babuni.dev · **Version:** 1.2.0 · **Game:** World of Warcraft Vanilla 1.12 · **Interface:** 11200 · **License:** [MIT](LICENSE)

**Group Buff Toggle** is a lightweight, Blizzard-style addon that places **up to 16 beneficial aura icons beside each of four default party-member frames** and, independently, **up to 16 beside the default target frame**. Two familiar **Buffs** checkboxes make those overlays easy to switch on or off. The checkboxes can also be independently hidden via slash commands.

**Both buff displays begin switched off**, so installing the addon does not immediately put new buff icons on the screen. Both checkbox-visibility preferences begin on, but a checkbox appears only while its corresponding party or target unit frame is available. The four switches are saved **account-wide**.

The addon *displays buffs only*. It does **not** apply, remove, prioritize, cast, dispel, track remaining durations, show debuffs as a separate list, or automatically choose a target.

## Install and enable

Copy the project folder so that the source and manifest are here:

```text
World of Warcraft/
└── Interface/
    └── AddOns/
        └── GroupBuffToggle/
            ├── GroupBuffToggle.toc
            └── GroupBuffToggle.lua
```

Restart WoW or run `/reload`. Enable **Group Buff Toggle** at character selection. The [published v1.2.0 release](https://github.com/babunidev/GroupBuffToggle/releases/tag/v1.2.0) provides [GroupBuffToggle.zip](https://github.com/babunidev/GroupBuffToggle/releases/download/v1.2.0/GroupBuffToggle.zip) and a SHA256SUMS text file. The release exists; its files were **not downloaded and checksum-verified in this documentation audit**.

The addon has no required external library and no configuration window. It is specifically built for **default Blizzard PartyMemberFrame1–4 and TargetFrame anchors**, not for substitute party/target frames from other UI addons.

## How to use it

With a party, tick **Buffs** below the lowest currently visible party frame to show member buffs in two eight-icon rows beside each displayed party member. Untick it to hide them. Select a target, then tick its separate **Buffs** checkbox to display that unit's buffs. Hover a buff icon for the native **GameTooltip**.

The checkboxes themselves appear only in context: the party control requires a visible, populated party frame; the target control requires a visible target frame with a target. A missing checkbox when solo or without a target does **not** mean the account setting has been lost.

### Four independent controls

| Saved key in `GroupBuffsDB` | Default | Command | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | **false** | `/groupbuffs group on\|off\|toggle` | Show/hide **party buff icons** |
| `groupCheckbox` | **true** | `/groupbuffs groupbox on\|off\|toggle` | Show/hide the **party Buffs checkbox** |
| `targetEnabled` | **false** | `/groupbuffs target on\|off\|toggle` | Show/hide **target buff icons** |
| `targetCheckbox` | **true** | `/groupbuffs targetbox on\|off\|toggle` | Show/hide the **target Buffs checkbox** |

Type `/groupbuffs` alone to see help and the status of all four controls. For example, `/groupbuffs group on` turns on party buffs, while `/groupbuffs groupbox off` hides only their checkbox. **Hiding a checkbox does not disable its buff icons**; slash controls still work.

Aliases accepted by the source: `party` for `group`; `groupcheckbox` or `partybox` for `groupbox`; `targetcheckbox` for `targetbox`. All take `on`, `off`, or `toggle` as a separate second argument. The addon does not register a separate `/targetbuffs` command.

The README previously said “stores only two settings,” but that described the initial display toggles; **current v1.2.0 code actually persists all four settings**. This source-based correction is part of the present documentation review.

## Buff layout and refresh

Each of four party rows and the target row is a **16-icon, two-row (8+8)** grid. Each icon is **20×20 px**, with **2 px** spacing. The party grid sits to the right of its corresponding frame, and the target grid also sits beside the normal target frame. The addon reads `UnitBuff("party1" .. "party4", index)` and `UnitBuff("target", index)` for **indices 1–16**, shows the texture when present, and hides an absent buff button.

It refreshes on `VARIABLES_LOADED`, `PLAYER_ENTERING_WORLD`, `PARTY_MEMBERS_CHANGED`, and `UNIT_AURA`, as well as a simple **0.5-second** periodic refresh. Tooltips use `GameTooltip:SetUnitBuff` with the unit and buff index. The code doesn't store item IDs, party/target names or a permanent buff history.

**Limits:** this is party-plus-target, **not raid-frame integration**; it shows buff textures, **not durations or charge overlays**. Stacks returned by `UnitBuff` are not rendered. A buff can appear or disappear with up to approximately a half-second timer delay in cases not covered by immediate events. Client and addon interoperability weren't independently tested in this audit.

## Upgrade from the old name: Octo Group Buff Toggle

The addon originally used folder/TOC **OctoGroupBuffToggle**, saved variable **OctoGroupBuffsDB** and title **Octo Group Buff Toggle**. The September 18 rename changed the folder/script and root variable. **Simply replacing files is not enough to recover an old SavedVariables file under its former name.**

1. Exit WoW completely and **back up your WTF SavedVariables folders**.
2. Install the new **GroupBuffToggle** folder beside the original **OctoGroupBuffToggle** directory.
3. On Windows/PowerShell, open the new addon folder and run:

```powershell
.\Upgrade-SavedData.ps1 -ClientPath "C:\Games\World of Warcraft" -PreviousAddonName "OctoGroupBuffToggle"
```

The helper reads the actual TOC declarations, finds saved files, copies backups to `AddonUpgradeBackups`, writes renamed copies without replacing any existing target file, and changes **only top-level** variable assignments from the old to new names. It does **not execute saved Lua** and leaves old files intact. Verify the copied settings, then disable the old addon. Do not run this while WoW is open.

On Linux, back up and manually copy the old `WTF/Account/.../SavedVariables/OctoGroupBuffToggle.lua` to the corresponding **GroupBuffToggle.lua**, and change the top-level assignment to **GroupBuffsDB**. Don't alter values inside the table; preserve the original until you verify the settings.

The [migration fixture](tests/test_upgrade.ps1) is present in the repository and simulates saved-data moves, backups, Unicode text and overwrite refusal. It **was not executed in this audit**.

The addon uses WoW 1.12-era frame names and old Lua callback conventions. Replacement unit-frame addons may move or remove those frames; their support is not claimed. No Lua/game client tests were performed during this documentation audit.

**Creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev. **Project:** Group Buff Toggle for WoW Vanilla 1.12.

## Put helpful information beside the people it describes

Buff icons usually live inside or around the game's unit-frame information hierarchy. When fighting alongside a party or watching a target, a player may want to know **which positive effects are active** without cramming more status information on top of the name, health and mana bars.

The project's concrete answer is a **small supplementary buff strip beside** each normal party frame and the selected target frame. Up to sixteen aura icons fit in two rows of eight, leaving the original frame readable. Hovering a symbol uses the familiar built-in game tooltip rather than introducing a separate interpretation layer.

This is deliberately not a complex raid frame, aura-warning assistant or combat automation system. No casts, prioritization, suggestions or warnings are authored; it simply makes current buffs easier to inspect when the player chooses to.

## Respect the existing UI until invited

An unusually valuable design constraint is present from the initial version: **both displays default to off**. Installing Group Buff Toggle should not dramatically change the player's screen by surprise. The controls are familiar native **Buffs** checkboxes, positioned only when a matching unit frame is present.

The September 10 second commit pushed user control further: **checkbox visibility itself** became independent from **the buff display**. A user could leave party buffs showing and hide the small toggle control for a cleaner layout—or turn everything off without leaving a permanently unused widget. That is a meaningful design refinement: the checkbox is an optional affordance, not the owner's source of truth.

The four switches persist account-wide. “Off by default” applies to **buff icons**, not to checkbox availability. That distinction is part of the authored user experience and shouldn't be blurred.

## Lightweight means bounded and local

The addon uses client `UnitBuff` data for a maximum of **four party members plus one target**, capped at **16 icons each**. It attaches to Blizzard's already-present `PartyMemberFrame1` through `4` and `TargetFrame`. It does not rebuild the frames, ask for an addon framework or create an external service.

The cost of that approach is limited compatibility with wholesale unit-frame replacements and a deliberately modest information set: aura **icons with hover details**, not timers, stack badges, or comprehensive raid support. These are limits of the current code, not promised future features.

## Identity and creative provenance

The repository started on September 10 as **Octo Group Buff Toggle**, aimed at an older Vanilla-compatible environment. The September 18 version changed to a provider-neutral title, `GroupBuffToggle`, and renamed its SavedVariables while retaining the small original interaction concept.

The MIT License makes reuse terms explicit, and its existing 2026 copyright notice now credits **Babuni.dev**. Git proves the dated code changes but does not reproduce the creator's original conversations or necessarily the author of every line. The original purpose and creative decisions belong to Babuni.dev; later AI source interpretation is separately credited in the collaboration record.

## The small engineering decisions supporting the gesture

The 303-line current Lua file demonstrates how much detail is needed to make a small visual addition feel as though it belongs to the game. For each party member the addon creates sixteen hoverable icon buttons and anchors their container just beyond the right edge of the default party frame. The target gets its own matching grid at an offset that fits beside Blizzard's target artwork.

The party checkbox doesn't float at a fixed world-screen coordinate. The source scans the party members from fourth down to first, finds the last visible populated frame and puts the checkbox just below that member. As the group grows, it moves with the list. The target checkbox follows the target frame and hides when there is no target.

The source refreshes on world entry, group changes and aura updates. A half-second periodic pass also rechecks frame visibility and position. This is a straightforward legacy-client solution: older addons have limited layout change signals, so polling ensures the display can recover from missed updates. It also creates repeated work even when nothing changed; performance should be assessed in a real client instead of assumed good or bad.

The icon-border texture uses a file named `UI-Debuff-Overlays`, which could mislead someone reading the name alone. The code's data path is `UnitBuff`: it shows **buffs**, not a separate debuff list. There are no aura duration numbers, charge overlays, timers, dispel hints, group-message logs or raid-unit panels. These absences are part of an honest source inventory, not evidence that features were intentionally rejected in an unavailable discussion.

# GroupBuffToggle — code architecture and runtime dataflow

**Audited:** `GroupBuffToggle.lua` (303 lines), `GroupBuffToggle.toc`, Git commits and migration scripts. October 27, 2026; **static review only**.

## Single-module package

```text
GroupBuffToggle.toc
  Interface: 11200 | Version: 1.2.0
  SavedVariables: GroupBuffsDB  (account-wide)
  GroupBuffToggle.lua
     ├─ default party and target frame references
     ├─ 4 party grids of 16 icon buttons
     ├─ 1 target grid of 16 icon buttons
     ├─ group + target Blizzard UICheckButtonTemplate controls
     ├─ event handling / 0.5-second polling
     └─ /groupbuffs command dispatch
```

There is no dependency/library, network synchronization, hidden targeting routine or alternative unit-frame abstraction. The source calls the built-in game's `UnitBuff` and `GameTooltip:SetUnitBuff` APIs.

## Default state and persistence

```text
GroupBuffsDB = {
  enabled = false,          -- party buff icons
  targetEnabled = false,    -- target buff icons
  groupCheckbox = true,     -- party checkbox affordance
  targetCheckbox = true     -- target checkbox affordance
}
```

On `VARIABLES_LOADED`, each key is populated **only if nil**, preserving saved user choices. The source doesn't restore default values on every login. This is an **account-wide** table declared as `SavedVariables`, not per-character. The previous README claimed only two settings, but the post-September-10 source has four.

`BuffsEnabled` and `TargetBuffsEnabled` require strict true; the checkbox-visibility functions require only **not false**, so missing checkbox keys behave as enabled even before initialization.

## Frame creation and placement

**Party:** for members 1–4, `CreateMemberBuffs` finds `PartyMemberFrameN`, then creates one container under `UIParent` anchored `TOPLEFT` to the party frame's `TOPRIGHT` with offset **(8,-4)**. Each container has 16 buttons, `MAX_BUFFS=16`; `ICONS_PER_ROW=8`, `ICON_SIZE=20`, `ICON_GAP=2`. Position of button i is computed using `math.mod(i-1,8)` for the column and `math.floor((i-1)/8)` for the row.

**Target:** one container anchored to `TargetFrame` `TOPRIGHT` at offset **(38,-18)**, also 16 icons in two rows. The target checkbox is positioned beside `TargetFrame` at offset **(4,-38)**. The party checkbox sits below the **highest-index visible, existing** party frame, found scanning member 4 down to 1, offset **(4,-6)** from its bottom-left.

The icons use native textures from `UnitBuff`, cropped via tex coords (0.07..0.93) and a subtle border texture from the game's `UI-Debuff-Overlays` sheet. That **border texture** does not make the displayed auras debuffs: the source only calls **UnitBuff**, not **UnitDebuff**.

## Refresh path and visibility

```text
VARIABLES_LOADED  -> initialize defaults, create checkboxes, UpdateAll
PLAYER_ENTERING_WORLD
PARTY_MEMBERS_CHANGED  ---> UpdateAll()
UNIT_AURA
OnUpdate every 0.5s ----> UpdateAll()

UpdateAll:
  for member in 1..4: UpdateMember(member)
  UpdateCheckboxPosition()
  UpdateTargetBuffs()
```

`UpdateMember` reparents position relative to the live party frame, then hides its container if party overlay disabled, unit doesn't exist, or the frame isn't shown. Otherwise each of the 16 slots calls `UnitBuff("partyN", index)`, sets the icon texture and visible state, and remembers the unit and buff index for hover.

`UpdateTargetBuffs` similarly hides its grid when target buff display disabled, target absent or `TargetFrame` hidden; its checkbox is visible only if `targetCheckbox` and target/frame visibility conditions all hold. It queries `UnitBuff("target", i)` only when enabled with a target.

**Important:** a visible checkbox flag isn't the same thing as enabled overlay. Hiding the checkbox leaves the overlay's independent saved flag unchanged.

If all four party and one target grid are visible, each full refresh can query up to **80 aura slots** (4×16 + 16) in addition to frame/checkbox work. Combined with a twice-per-second poll this is **up to about 160 periodic UnitBuff queries per second**, excluding event-triggered updates. This is a theoretical source-level maximum, **not** a measured performance result.

## Hover and update semantics

Party buttons set `button.unit="partyN"` and `buffIndex=i` when a buff is found; target buttons set their unit/index at frame creation. On hover, `GameTooltip:SetUnitBuff(this.unit,this.buffIndex)` displays the native buff tooltip; on leave it hides the tooltip.

The addon currently displays **only icons**, not remaining duration, stacks, source player, dispellability or buffs beyond the 16th. It has no persistent aura log or personal data collection mechanism.

On each periodic refresh the source adjusts positions and current buff icon visibility, but it doesn't replace default party/target frame internals. Custom unit-frame addons that remove those named frames won't be supported by this code without adaptation.

## Commands

The sole registered slash command is `/groupbuffs`. After trimming/lowercasing, its parser expects two tokens: **control** and **on/off/toggle**.

| Control aliases | Saved key |
| --- | --- |
| `group`, `party` | `enabled` |
| `groupbox`, `groupcheckbox`, `partybox` | `groupCheckbox` |
| `target` | `targetEnabled` |
| `targetbox`, `targetcheckbox` | `targetCheckbox` |

Invalid or empty messages print syntax and current state. Valid commands modify one key, print new state, update visible checkbox checks and call `UpdateAll`.

## Migration, licensing and test limits

September 18 changed old **OctoGroupBuffToggle** identity and root variable **OctoGroupBuffsDB** to **GroupBuffToggle / GroupBuffsDB**. `Upgrade-SavedData.ps1` maps old/new TOC variable names, copies source to backups, rewrites only root assignments in newly created files and refuses overwrites. A separate `tests/test_upgrade.ps1` fixture builds synthetic temporary SavedVariables trees to check Unicode, backups, original retention and refusal behavior.

The repository includes **MIT LICENSE** with Babuni.dev copyright and [v1.2.0 release](https://github.com/babunidev/GroupBuffToggle/releases/tag/v1.2.0) with ZIP/checksum files. Historic release notes **report** syntax/migration verification. Neither game-client validation nor execution of scripts was performed in this review.

# GroupBuffToggle — interface and interaction design

**Creative director:** Babuni.dev. **Evidence:** original README, current code and the two September 10 commits.

## A native UI affordance, not another configuration window

The addon uses Blizzard's familiar **UICheckButtonTemplate** and a small **Buffs** label placed where players are already looking: below their visible party frame stack and beside their current target. No new floating options panel, media bundle or unfamiliar controls are required.

The content sits **to the right** of existing unit frames, so health and resource bars aren't covered. Four possible party grids and one target grid each have two rows of eight small icons (16 total per unit). Buff buttons can be hovered for familiar native tooltips. This uses the game visual language rather than inventing a new type of aura graphic.

## Opt-in by default

A central design decision is that **buff overlays default off**. The user must tick a checkbox or enable a slash setting to alter the information density of the game UI. The checkboxes can be offered when units exist, even if the overlay itself is currently off.

This small restraint is significant. Unit frames are already visually busy; adding 16 icons for each member without invitation might create a disruptive change. The creator's solution keeps the new information available but doesn't insist on showing it.

## The September 10 interaction refinement

The first version had only two persistent visibility flags for party and target buffs. The same-day **“Add independent slash controls”** revision introduced two additional settings controlling **the visibility of the checkboxes**. The player can choose to show buffs while removing the toggle itself, or keep the control present but leave the icons hidden.

That creates four independent states rather than two, with clear direct `/groupbuffs` commands to access each. It is an example of making a small interface less intrusive through a second design pass rather than making it larger.

## Context matters for placement

The party checkbox follows the **last visible party-member frame** in the normal vertical stack; there is no party checkbox when no appropriate unit frame exists. The target checkbox follows the target frame and is shown only when a target exists. These rules keep controls from floating around the screen unattached to any subject.

The icon grids also hide when their corresponding units or Blizzard frames aren't shown. Each refresh reanchors positions to the currently available frames, supporting changing roster layouts within the default UI.

## Visual details and limits

Each buff icon is **20 px**, with a small **2 px** gap, cropped to remove empty texture edges and shown with a quiet gray border. The code uses a native texture sheet named `UI-Debuff-Overlays` as a *decorative frame*, but does not query debuffs. No durations, stacks, counters, expiration effects, sorting or aura type labels are currently drawn.

The amount and placement of information is intentionally fixed; an expanded raid layout would be a separate approved feature, not a small styling tweak.

## Future tests, not design claims

The icon-only layout should be examined at low resolutions, large UI scales, for color-vision accessibility, and with other buffs already present around unit frames. Check whether the target grid overlaps default status elements and whether tooltip hit areas remain easy to use. No screenshot or game-client usability test is in the current repo, and none was conducted during this audit.

## Tradeoffs visible in current design

**Checkbox vs icon-overlay independence.** Hiding the control does not hide the data. This supports minimalist UI arrangements but can be confusing unless documented. The README is corrected accordingly.

**Defaults.** The two buff displays default off, so install doesn't unexpectedly fill the screen. Checkbox visibility defaults on only when unit-frame context exists.

**Fixed native anchors.** Placing content near Blizzard party/target frames is simple and natural but creates a compatibility boundary with custom unit-frame replacements.

**Fixed 16-icon cap.** Two rows of eight produce predictable geometry. Additional buffs, stacks and expiry information are not shown.

**Event + 0.5s poll.** Occasional polling protects against events/visibility changes that don't arrive as expected in old clients, but means regular periodic work even when content is unchanged.

**Account-wide settings.** Same four preferences apply to every character; separate character profiles aren't part of today's design.

**Open source under MIT.** Unlike repositories missing licenses, this addon intentionally includes MIT terms. Current notice credits Babuni.dev; its legal terms are not to be silently altered by an AI collaborator.

Unlike a curated combat-addon whitelist, this addon **does not store names or icons for individual spells**. It queries the current game client's **UnitBuff** textures for five possible units:

| Unit token | Vanilla frame anchor | Cap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `party1` | `PartyMemberFrame1` | 16 buffs |
| `party2` | `PartyMemberFrame2` | 16 buffs |
| `party3` | `PartyMemberFrame3` | 16 buffs |
| `party4` | `PartyMemberFrame4` | 16 buffs |
| `target` | `TargetFrame` | 16 buffs |

The game supplies textures, their order and the tooltip returned for the unit/index. The addon doesn't generate individual buff names, build a spell database, communicate with the party or log aura history.

## Authored controls and text

- The two checkboxes use the simple label **Buffs**.
- Party checkbox tooltip: **Group Buffs**, explaining party-member buffs beside group frames.
- Target checkbox tooltip: **Target Buffs**, explaining buffs beside the target frame.
- Chat command prefix uses **Group Buffs:** and shows command status.
- Slash help displays `group`, `groupbox`, `target`, `targetbox` with `on|off|toggle` choices.

The names are English literals, but individual buff tooltips come from the game. The project contains **no localization directory** or translated settings UI.

`GroupBuffsDB`, account-wide:

| Field | Initial value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |

| `targetEnabled` | false | Target buff grid visible when appropriate |
| `groupCheckbox` | true | Show contextual party Buffs checkbox |

# GuildChatBridge

**Creative direction:** Babuni  
**Status:** Paused experiment; not a functioning AI character

GuildChatBridge began with a roleplaying idea: what if my World of Warcraft character could have a voice of their own? While I controlled movement, combat and other actions, a local AI could notice what happened around the character, interpret guild conversation and occasionally speak in character. The aim was not a gameplay bot. It was an experiment in giving a player-controlled character a second, partly independent social life.

The first ambition was an AI that could read guild chat and respond there without my composing every line. Later possibilities included reactions to crafting, fighting, loot and nearby events, with party or raid conversations as possible extensions. The character should speak when something mattered to them, not fill every silence.

## Why the project is paused

The original attempt stalled because I could not complete the automatic conversation loop with the tools and access available to me. At the time, I understood sending chat to require direct player input, and did not want to rely on unsupported or intrusive workarounds.

That explanation needs one technical qualification: `SendChatMessage` exists, and this prototype itself calls it for guild chat. Available API references and examples of 1.12-era addons show that automatic chat transmission is not categorically impossible. What remains unsolved here is a **reliable, permitted, live connection between game events, an external AI and in-game speech**, including the rules of the particular server. No autonomous response loop is implemented or verified. See [architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) and [decisions](docs/DECISIONS.md).

The idea remains on ice rather than abandoned. An AI that *suggests* character-appropriate lines for me to choose from is a possible future direction, not an implemented feature or a decision to resume development. A separate roleplaying-assistant concept should not be confused with this project.

## What the repository actually contains

The installed addon still uses its original name, **GuildChatAI**. Its Lua source attempts to:

- Capture `CHAT_MSG_GUILD` messages and guild-roster names in `GuildChatAIDB`.
- Print received messages to the chat frame.
- Send text manually supplied through `/gcai <message>` using `SendChatMessage(msg, "GUILD")`.

It does **not** include an AI model, external process, network bridge, generated dialogue, automatic replies or activity-based personality. The code has not been verified in a live client during these documentation reviews.

### Installation snapshot — unverified

The source layout suggests placing `GuildChatAI.lua` and `GuildChatAI.toc` inside `Interface/AddOns/GuildChatAI/`. The manifest declares interface `11200`. Actual 1.12 compatibility and loading behavior still require testing. The slash command sends user-provided text, not AI output.

The repository name changed from `GuildChatAI` to `GuildChatBridge` on October 31, 2026. Lua and TOC filenames, `GuildChatAIDB` and `/gcai` were intentionally left unchanged.

# GuildChatBridge — concept

**Creative:** Babuni  
**Stage:** Paused exploration

## A character with a life of their own

The idea came from enjoying roleplay while wondering whether the character could contribute more than the actions and words I explicitly chose. In the experiment I imagined, the player would still steer the character through Azeroth, but an AI would shape their conversational voice.

Guild chat was the starting point. The character could follow discussions, decide whether something interested them and respond in their own manner. Through game events, they might notice crafting, combat, items collected or changes in the surrounding world. Those observations could become small opinions, stories or remarks. Party and raid chat were possible later extensions, not established features.

The desired feeling was closer to an AI-driven NPC sharing a player's journey than a conventional command-based chatbot. Yet this was never intended to transfer gameplay control to the AI: movement and actions would remain mine.

## The interesting boundary

A character that speaks independently might feel alive, but one that talks too much, interrupts players or impersonates genuine human attention could quickly become unwelcome. Part of the experiment was finding the narrow space where that behavior might be playful and respectful of the people sharing the game.

Meaningful silence matters as much as speech. The imagined character would have interests and context rather than simply reply to every guild message. Any future design needs transparent AI participation and should respect server rules, consent, chat volume and the ability to disable responses.

## Why it stopped, and why it remains

The original vision required an end-to-end loop: observe the game, bring the observations to an AI, let the AI decide what to say and deliver the result in game. The attempt did not achieve that loop, and I set it aside rather than claim it worked or force a workaround I did not want.

The belief that all guild-chat output necessarily requires keyboard confirmation should not be treated as a proven 1.12 API rule. Chat sending exists in the source; external AI communication, real-time observation and server permission are separate unresolved problems.

A less autonomous version, in which an AI offers roleplay lines for me to send, remains a **possible direction only**. The separate roleplaying helper concept is not part of GuildChatBridge.

## Evidence

This creative account was supplied by me on October 31, 2026, after the original prototype. The repository proves that logging and a manual-send command were written; it does not prove that the imagined AI behavior was implemented, tested or approved for a server. See [the journal](docs/DEVLOG.md) and [architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md).

# GuildChatBridge — architecture and technical limits

## Existing implementation

The repository contains `GuildChatAI.lua` and `GuildChatAI.toc`, not an external AI application. The manifest declares interface `11200` and account-wide `GuildChatAIDB`.

The Lua source creates a frame, registers `ADDON_LOADED`, `CHAT_MSG_GUILD` and `GUILD_ROSTER_UPDATE`, and attempts the following:

| Path | Observed code | Not established |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Guild messages | Appends timestamp, sender and message to `guildMessages`; prints a copy | Persistent disk chat logging or successful client execution |
| Guild roster | Clears and repopulates a name-to-true map via guild-roster functions | Stable event behavior or complete member metadata |
| Manual send | `/gcai <message>` calls `SendChatMessage(msg, "GUILD")` | Delivery acknowledgement or AI-composed text |
| Saved data | Uses `GuildChatAIDB` declared in the TOC | Safe initialization for every client/load order, retention or migration |

No network client, localhost API, model invocation, event-to-model queue, character memory, generation prompts or autonomous sending loop exists in this source. Capturing text in an addon is not equivalent to transmitting it to a local application.

## Why the intended end-to-end system is unfinished

A future implementation would need three independently working stages:

1. **Observation:** Collect only events exposed by the intended client (guild or group messages and relevant activities).
2. **AI bridge:** Transfer selected observations to a local model promptly through a supported, permitted route, then receive a response.
3. **Expression:** Show a proposed line to the player or transmit it in an allowed channel, with rate and consent controls.

These are **conceptual components**, not implemented modules. Standard SavedVariables write on logout/reload rather than serving as a continuously updated external message stream. A client addon also should not be assumed to have arbitrary file, socket or HTTP access. Both directions of any external bridge require actual verification.

## Important correction about chat sending

The existing code contains `SendChatMessage(msg, "GUILD")`. Modern WoW API documentation distinguishes guild/party/raid chat from channels requiring hardware interaction, and historical 1.12.1 addon examples describe timer-based chat messages. Thus `all in-game chat requires Enter or paste` is not a reliable general rule. Neither those references nor this source establish permission or success for a fully automatic AI character on the intended realm.

References: [SendChatMessage API](https://warcraft.wiki.gg/wiki/API_SendChatMessage), [1.12.1 automatic-message addon example](https://github.com/0ldi/AutoMessage), [SavedVariables lifecycle](https://warcraft.wiki.gg/wiki/Saved_variables).

## Client-compatibility and correctness checks

- The legacy 1.12 client uses Lua 5.0 conventions; inspect event callback parameters and `...` usage rather than assuming modern `self, event, ...` behavior.
- Check saved-variable initialization at `ADDON_LOADED`, including preexisting/malformed tables.
- Check `date("%m/%d %H:%M:%S.%f")`: fractional seconds are not safely assumed supported.
- Test whether invoking `GuildRoster()` from `GUILD_ROSTER_UPDATE` causes excess updates.
- Verify guild presence, chat permission, throttling, error handling and whether the apparent send confirmation corresponds to actual delivery.
- Set a retention/deletion policy before retaining other players' chat logs for prolonged periods.

The code was inspected as text; no in-game or automated compatibility test was run during this documentation revision.

# GuildChatBridge — intended experience

## The imagined interaction

During ordinary gameplay, I would continue making the decisions that move my character through the world. Their voice, however, might develop its own small life. Guildmates could be chatting while the character noticed something relevant, formed an opinion and occasionally joined the conversation in character.

Crafting, combat and loot were examples of context the AI might use, not features already captured by the addon. Guild chat was the main setting; party and raid channels were possible expansions.

The distinction from a traditional chatbot is important: the character would not simply answer every incoming message. Context, personality and selective interest were central to the intended illusion.

## What the current addon feels like

The code does something much smaller. It collects guild-message text and names, prints captured messages and offers `/gcai` to send text typed by the player. There is no character voice, contextual awareness, UI for proposed dialogue, or AI interaction. This interaction has not been tested in the intended game client during the documentation review.

## Boundaries for any redesign

The most interesting design challenge is also the social risk. An autonomous roleplayed character should not bury guild conversations, confuse people about who is speaking or continue when the player wants silence.

Ideas worth investigating, **not approved features**, include clear disclosure, channel selection, conservative response frequency, a prominent off control and a manual suggestion mode. Automatic publishing must be considered separately from generating interesting text. Technical feasibility alone would not settle whether the result belongs in a shared game.

This project concerns the character speaking in guild and group life; a separate roleplaying speech assistant is not a replacement for this concept.

# LevelUpAnnouncer — architecture

**By:** Babuni

`LevelMessages` maps integers 1 through 60 to fixed English strings. `PreviewLevel` prints locally; `AnnounceLevelToGuild` checks `IsInGuild()` before `SendChatMessage`. Both use a generic fallback when no exact table key exists.

A frame registers `PLAYER_ENTERING_WORLD` and `PLAYER_LEVEL_UP`. Entering the world sets `BuxbrewDing_LastLevel` to the player's current level without announcing. The level-up branch uses numeric `arg1`, falling back to `UnitLevel`, and sends only when the new level exceeds the tracked one and is at most 60. It advances the tracked level even if the player is not in a guild.

The slash handler trims text, calls `string.match`, lowercases the command and routes previews or sends. Its manual-send branch prints “Announced” after calling the helper, even when the helper declined for lack of guild membership. It does not update the automatic event tracker. No automated tests exist in the inspected tree.

Despite comments calling the global a saved variable, the TOC has no SavedVariables declaration. Entering-world initialization further means this is an in-session duplicate guard, not evidence of a durable announcement ledger.

# Loot Feed

**Author:** Babuni.dev

A compact, movable loot feed for **World of Warcraft 1.12**. No dependencies.

- Five animated loot rows with item icons, rarity colors, and stack counts.
- Copper, silver, and gold icons, plus a gold **Quest Item** label for quest items.
- Hover to pause the feed and see item tooltips.
- Group rolls stay visible with a dice tooltip showing names, Need/Greed/Pass choices, numbers, and the winner.
- Adjustable position, size, duration, and stack direction.

## Install

Download the published [v0.2.2 LootFeed.zip](https://github.com/babunidev/LootFeed/releases/download/v0.2.2/LootFeed.zip), extract the `LootFeed` folder into `Interface\AddOns`, and restart WoW. Enable **Loot Feed** at character select.

## Upgrade from a previous add-on name

If you used this add-on under a previous folder name, migrate your saved data
before playing with the new installation. A normal file replacement is not
enough when the folder and saved-variable names change.

1. Fully close the game. Keep the previous add-on installed for this step.
2. Install the new `LootFeed` folder beside the previous folder.
3. Open PowerShell in `LootFeed` and run the following, replacing both example values:

   ```powershell
   .\Upgrade-SavedData.ps1 -ClientPath "C:\Games\World of Warcraft" -PreviousAddonName "PreviousAddonFolder"
   ```

The helper reads the previous TOC, copies account-wide and per-character saved
data to the new names, and saves backups under `AddonUpgradeBackups` in the
game folder. It keeps the original files intact and refuses to overwrite
existing saved data for the new add-on. It does not execute saved Lua code.

4. Disable the previous add-on and enable **LootFeed** before entering the world.
5. Check your settings and saved data. Keep the backups until you have verified them.

Further updates using the same add-on name keep your saved data normally.
On other operating systems, back up the files, then copy the previous add-on's
`.lua` file in each `WTF/Account/**/SavedVariables` directory to `LootFeed.lua`.
Change only the top-level variable name declared in the old TOC to the matching
name in the new TOC; leave its table contents unchanged. Do this with the game closed.

## Commands

- `/lfeed unlock` — drag into position; `/lfeed lock` to finish.
- `/lfeed test` — preview the feed.
- `/lfeed testroll` — preview a group roll; hover the dice as it progresses.
- `/lfeed scale 1` — adjust size.
- `/lfeed duration 6` — seconds before fading.
- `/lfeed direction up` or `down` — change stack direction.
- `/lfeed chat off` — hide personal item loot in chat; `chat on` restores it.
- `/lfeed reset` — restore defaults.

Settings are saved account-wide. Quest labels follow the item's tooltip; ordinary materials needed for quests are not marked.

Group rolls use the normal game's Need/Greed/Pass buttons. Active rolls add rows
as needed and stay until resolved; results remain for 15 seconds, paused while
hovering. The winner appears beside the dice. Detailed loot messages
(`showLootSpam`) are enabled to receive everyone's choices and rolls. Players
whose choice has not been received are shown as waiting/eligibility unknown.
If identical items are rolled simultaneously, Vanilla's chat cannot distinguish
the copies; the tooltip reports that limitation instead of guessing. Missing
results time out explicitly without inventing a winner. Rolls in progress before
the add-on loads cannot be reconstructed.

## What the source actually does

The installed addon folder is **LootFeed**, with **LootFeed.toc**, **Rolls.lua** and **LootFeed.lua**. The TOC declares interface **11200**, version **0.2.2** and account-wide SavedVariables **LootFeedDB**. The interface registers **/lfeed** and **/lootfeed** as equivalent aliases.

**Ordinary loot:** the five-row limit applies to *normal* item and money notifications. Incoming identical item links can be coalesced while still in the queue, but items already visible are not merged away. Entries animate in, slide to their new stack position, then fade after the selected delay (default **6 seconds**, adjustable from **2–20 seconds**). New rows are inserted no more frequently than about **0.32 seconds**. When ordinary rows are full, the oldest is expired rather than allowing an unlimited stack.

**Group rolls:** roll rows are **extra** and may exceed those five normal rows. They remain displayed while unresolved and can show **Need / Greed / Pass**, reported numbers and eventual winner. On completion, the row remains for around **15 seconds** before fading; hover pauses the visible feed timer. This is session-only roll tracking, **not a permanent saved history of group decisions**. The roll tracker itself retains completed records internally for up to **300 seconds** to handle delayed messages.

The dice are drawn by the addon as a tiny five-pip symbol rather than requiring an external image. Hover the dice for the participant breakdown. The normal Blizzard Need/Greed/Pass window remains in control of the player's actual roll.

**Important interaction side effect:** when the client setting `showLootSpam` is `0`, `Rolls.lua` sets it to `1` so detailed choice and number messages become available. The addon does **not** restore the previous value when switched off/unloaded. Likewise, `/lfeed chat off` wraps the legacy global `ChatFrame_OnEvent` handler to hide recognized **personal item** messages in chat. It does not suppress money messages or group-roll tracking. Review compatibility with other chat-handler addons if both are installed.

**Limits:** the self-loot parser uses the client's `LOOT_ITEM_*` string formats; the roll parser uses `LOOT_ROLL_*` templates with positional placeholder support. Full localized/custom-server behavior is not independently proven. Quest Item detection checks for the binding text on the actual item tooltip; **quest-needed materials** lacking that text are not labeled. A loot item may arrive before `GetItemInfo` finishes caching, so the display retries an item refresh.

# LootFeed — creative concept

**Original creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev.  
**Game-client target:** original World of Warcraft 1.12 (TOC 11200).  
**Historical identity:** Octo Loot → Loot Feed.

## Giving rewards a moment on screen

LootFeed is a small interface experiment about **the feeling of getting something**. The ordinary game chat tells a player what was looted, but that information is easy to lose while traveling, fighting and talking. This addon makes those moments briefly visible in a **compact stack of softly animated notifications**. Rarity colors, item art, quantities, money denominations and genuine quest-item labels are placed close together without taking over the game.

The default design has **five short rows for regular loot**, set against a dark translucent backing, with a small entrance pop, smooth vertical movement and a fade-out. The player can move the anchor, choose direction and adjust scale and duration. **Hovering pauses** the stack so an item can be inspected. It is a deliberately temporary visual memory, not an inventory manager or an item database.

The initial September 8 release already carried this visual identity. The exact original brainstorming conversations are not present in the inspected Git history; Babuni.dev retains authorship of the creative direction. This document describes the result rather than inventing an origin scene.

## From receiving loot to understanding group decisions

On September 11 the addon expanded beyond **personal** loot. A group Need/Greed/Pass roll is a shared decision whose details often disappear into the combat or chat stream. LootFeed added **extra, longer-lived roll rows** with a small drawn die. Hovering the die reveals names, choices and roll numbers; once the outcome arrives, the winner is shown directly on the row.

This is an important change in scope. Five short personal notifications are a stream. Roll decisions need **state over time** and sometimes more than five visible rows. Rather than replacing Blizzard's buttons or triggering a roll for the player, LootFeed observes the game's roll events and messages, preserving the player's agency.

## Make uncertainty visible

Vanilla loot chat contains an item link but not a unique roll identifier for every identical concurrent drop. The implementation does not pretend to match a player's response to one indistinguishable copy. It marks those cases as **ambiguous** in the tooltip.

Similarly, a missing winner does not justify inventing one. The row can say **“Ended (result unavailable)”** when the original deadline is exceeded. If a late genuine result arrives, that status is **provisional** and may be updated. When a local roll prompt closes, that is not automatically evidence that the group has completed the roll.

The small interface thus carries a broader creative principle: **give the player useful feedback without claiming knowledge the client does not provide**.

## The project's boundaries

LootFeed doesn't auto-roll, compare another player's fairness, rank loot recipients, redistribute items, or save an archival database of group behavior. It uses old-client Lua UI primitives and optional local chat hiding, with all remaining item/roll decisions made through normal game UI.

Potential improvements—reduced motion, more localization or different roll privacy—remain options for Babuni.dev rather than approved changes. The portfolio should show this as a compact interaction-design work, not expand it into a conventional loot-management dashboard without permission.

# LootFeed — the creative and technical development journal

**Original creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Retrospective prepared:** October 26, 2026. Evidence: current README, TOC, both Lua source files, PowerShell migration utility and test, screenshots, dated Git diffs and v0.2.2 release metadata. This is **not a transcript of every earlier conversation**; unknown motives are labeled rather than invented.

## Beginning with a small reward moment

The idea embodied in LootFeed is that picking up an item should be a pleasant, legible moment rather than another easy-to-miss chat message. The game's inventory system already knows what a player owns; this addon was designed to show the **event of receiving** something, briefly and clearly, while the player continues adventuring.

Its initial identity was **Octo Loot**. The first substantive Git commit, **`dde82cb8130f`** on September 8, 2026, was already described as a **0.1.5 release**. It came with one Lua source file, a 1.12 TOC, a concise README and three screenshots. That is the earliest preserved committed state, not proof that the entire idea and all of its design trials were completed in one sitting. Earlier creator dialogue or local test sessions were not recovered in the repository review.

The interface at that point was intentionally compact. There were **five small rows**, each able to display an item texture, colored name and stack count; money had a coin icon, and genuine Quest Items could receive a gold secondary label. These rows appeared with a modest scale/pop and moved into a stack before fading after a short duration. Hovering both paused the messages and surfaced the native item tooltip.

The original design offered player-controlled location, scale, lifetime and whether the stack builds up or down. A tiny green drag handle became visible only when unlocked. The appeal is in *reducing friction*: a player can keep playing, and each useful pickup remains momentarily intelligible.

Several small technical details express that direction. An item icon may not be cached when the item chat event arrives, so the UI retries `GetItemInfo` later rather than permanently displaying a question mark. Identical item links are combined **while waiting in the queue**, but an already displayed row retains its own short history. A Quest Item is detected by reading its tooltip's binding text, not by guessing whether a material is used by some quest.

Even the money icon tells a story about working within old client resources. Source comments say the developer visually inspected the Vanilla interface MPQ coin icons and selected different item textures for copper, silver and gold. This is historical technical evidence, not an independent repeat of that inspection in October.

## September 11 — a quick personal feed becomes group-aware

A few days later, commit **`fbbd50fac74d`**, “Add persistent group-roll entries with live dice tooltips,” expanded the addon from brief *personal loot* into a window on a **shared decision**.

A group Need/Greed/Pass roll cannot be represented well by one fading item notification. The roll remains in progress while several players make choices, sometimes while numerical results arrive later. A new **Rolls.lua** module appeared, handling roll start/cancel events, item-link keyed chat messages, participants, choices, numbers, winners and the possibility that results simply never appear.

The UI gained **additional roll rows** beyond its five ordinary rows. Each had a die drawn directly through Lua, with a small tooltip enumerating the players. The design left Blizzard's actual rolling buttons intact. LootFeed watched and explained a collective activity; it did not decide Need or Greed on the player's behalf.

This feature introduced an important technical dependency of a different kind: the addon needs detailed loot-roll chat. Its `Rolls.Init` enables the game CVar `showLootSpam` when disabled. There is no bundled library requirement, but there **is** a user-setting side effect. The current source does not save/restore the previous setting. This is a review item the portfolio should preserve rather than assuming it was consciously approved in all circumstances.

The source parses the game's own `LOOT_ROLL_*` localized templates, including numbered positional placeholders. Yet those messages still identify a player and item link without a stable ID for **which instance of an identical item** is being rolled. When two identical drops are up simultaneously, the addon declines to invent assignments and marks the outcome ambiguous. Unknown participant choices remain “Waiting / eligibility unknown.”

The developer created a **/oloot testroll** preview (now **/lfeed testroll**) that simulates ExampleMage and ExampleRogue choices. It is clearly labeled as a preview, offering a lightweight way to inspect the die/tooltips without asking a group of real players to run a test.

## Later September 11 — a bug in what “finished” meant

The second September 11 commit, **`86036564974e`**, is an especially revealing piece of development history. Its message was “Keep tracking group rolls after the local prompt closes.”

The initial roll handling had treated closing the *local* UI prompt as evidence of approaching group completion, with a short cancellation grace period. That assumption was too broad. The game's prompt can close for one player while choices and results are still traveling through the group.

The new code records `promptClosed` without making the roll done. It waits for **a genuine winner message, everyone passing, or the original deadline**. If the deadline arrives without proof, the record enters **Ended (result unavailable)** rather than assigning a fictional winner.

Even that status isn't necessarily the final word. A late authentic result can correct an earlier provisional timeout, while delayed numeric rolls may still arrive after a winner. The source retains completed records for a bounded time and refreshes the visual row when the status changes.

This is a concrete correction of an earlier implementation hypothesis. The commit demonstrates the code change; it doesn't reveal an entire debugging dialogue, a particular user's complaint, or a successful in-game reenactment. Keeping the distinction protects the project's true history while still explaining why the present solution exists.

## September 18 — changing names without losing the player's settings

Commit **`6126df1f90d7`**, “Use provider-neutral names and client compatibility descriptions,” renamed **Octo Loot** to **Loot Feed**, the project to `LootFeed`, the Lua globals, frame/TOC identifiers and account-wide saved variable from **OctoLootDB** to **LootFeedDB**. # LootFeed — architecture and roll-state guarantees

**Source inspected:** `LootFeed.lua` (316 lines), `Rolls.lua` (190 lines), manifest, migration helper and fixture, October 26, 2026. **Static review only**; no game or PowerShell test executed.

## Installed package

```text
LootFeed.toc   Interface 11200, Version 0.2.2
               SavedVariables: LootFeedDB (account-wide)
               Rolls.lua -> LootFeed.lua
Rolls.lua      LootFeedRolls global; roll records, message parser, timeouts
LootFeed.lua   feed rows, queue, icons, tooltip, animation, chat hook, commands
```

The TOC actually lists **Rolls.lua** first, then **LootFeed.lua**. The game uses the Vanilla-style globals `event`, `arg1` and `this`; no modern loot-history API, external library or server endpoint is required.

## Normal loot and money pipeline

```text
ADDON_LOADED ("LootFeed")
  -> LootFeedDB defaults and scale/duration clamps
  -> compile client LOOT_ITEM_* personal loot patterns
  -> make 5 normal UI row frames
  -> LootFeedRolls.Init(callback)
  -> Place() + lock anchor
  -> wrap original ChatFrame_OnEvent if available

CHAT_MSG_LOOT
  -> also pass into LootFeedRolls.Event for roll parsing
  -> if personal LOOT_ITEM_* match, extract item link / quantity
  -> Enqueue(item)

CHAT_MSG_MONEY
  -> parse localized denominations, select coin icon
  -> Enqueue(money text)

OnUpdate (every frame)
  -> LootFeedRolls.Tick()
  -> inject demos at ~0.7s spacing if active
  -> if hovering, pause visible stack and insertion
  -> expire and animate rows
  -> insert queue at >=0.32s spacing
  -> place/fade current rows
```

`Enqueue` coalesces **identical item links only among queued entries** by summing their quantity; items already active retain their separate display history. The standard `LIMIT=5` covers **non-roll** rows. When full, the oldest normal row is pushed into expiration, preserving the finite on-screen flow. Roll rows are not counted against the ordinary limit; they can create additional frames.

Rows use **270×40** logical dimensions, **5px** gap and a `0.9` compact scale layered onto the user scale. `LootFeedDB.duration` defaults **6s** and is clamped to **2–20s**; scale defaults 1 and is clamped **0.6–1.8**. Entrance pop runs around **0.32s**, fade around **0.7s**, while ordinary insertion is spaced by **0.32s**. Stack position eases toward the target. Up/down direction inverts the offsets.

`GetItemInfo` may be temporarily uncached. The renderer falls back to link text/known icons and retries refresh about every **0.5 seconds** until the texture resolves.

## Item and quest recognition

The source compiles six original `LOOT_ITEM_*` client string constants for self-loot and extracts `|Hitem:...|h` links. This compiler recognizes `%s` and `%d` substitutions but **does not** implement the positional-template mapping present in Rolls.lua, so language/provider support is not uniformly guaranteed.

Quest Item status is determined by scanning an actual `GameTooltip` and matching a line exactly to `ITEM_BIND_QUEST` (or the English fallback). That does **not** mean an ordinary item needed for a quest gets labeled.

Money text is normalized into copper, then picks a coin icon: total >= **10000** → gold, >= **100** → silver, otherwise copper. The note in source says the specific old-client coin icon paths were visually inspected from a client MPQ; this historical code comment does **not** count as new independent validation today.

## Group rolls as stateful records

```text
LootFeedRolls.records[id] = {
  id, link, item key, texture, amount,
  players[name] = { name, choice?, number? },
  order = [participant names],
  status, deadline, done?, winner?, finished?,
  promptClosed?, ambiguous?
}
LootFeedRolls.pending[id] = { duration, untilTime } # if link missing initially
```

The tracker receives `START_LOOT_ROLL`, `CANCEL_LOOT_ROLL` and `CHAT_MSG_LOOT`. On start, it asks `GetLootRollItemLink` and `GetLootRollItemInfo`, then takes an initial participant list from party or raid unit names. A roll with no item link is retried for **three seconds**; once resolved, the deadline is its supplied duration in milliseconds converted to seconds plus **15 seconds**.

`Rolls.Init` compiles client `LOOT_ROLL_*` format strings, including positional `%s`/`%d` placeholders. It also sets `showLootSpam=1` when the value is 0 so choices/numeric rolls are available in chat. The code does not revert that setting later.

For each matched message, the tracker searches for a **single unresolved matching item link**. Vanilla chat does not attach a unique roll ID to every chat choice. If multiple roll records share the link, it marks them ambiguous instead of attaching the message to one arbitrarily.

`CANCEL_LOOT_ROLL` sets **promptClosed** but **does not** declare a result. The group may still be rolling. A “winner” or “everyone passed” message completes the roll; otherwise the original deadline produces **Ended (result unavailable)**, with no invented winner. A genuine later result can update that provisional completion; delayed numeric outcomes may also arrive after a winner. Completed roll records are purged after **300 seconds**.

The UI callback `RollChanged` allocates an extra row if needed, draws a five-pip die, and refreshes a hover tooltip with participant status, numbers, winner or explicit ambiguity. While unresolved, row.age is held near the entrance value; once complete, the roll row displays around **15 seconds**, then fades. Hover pauses the **visible feed**, but `LootFeedRolls.Tick` still processes external roll events before the hover pause.

`/lfeed testroll` creates a **clearly labeled demo roll** with fictional ExampleMage/ExampleRogue members, not a real network action.

## Chat handler integration and risk

Vanilla lacks modern `ChatFrame_AddMessageEventFilter`. `LootFeed.lua` stores the current `ChatFrame_OnEvent` global and replaces it with a delegate that suppresses **recognized personal item CHAT_MSG_LOOT** only when `LootFeedDB.mute` is true. Other chat messages delegate to the prior function. Other addons may also wrap that global; load order, handler replacement and lifecycle need real client compatibility tests. Hiding loot in chat does **not** stop the feed recording it or stop group roll data.

Settings persisted: **x, y, scale, duration, direction, mute** in account-wide `LootFeedDB`. **Roll history is session-memory only.**

# LootFeed — interface and interaction design

**Creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev.

## A small celebration that doesn't become a second inventory

The feed is meant to be **noticed briefly**, not always visible. Standard entries are dark, compact rows that show a recognisable item icon, rarity-colored title and stack count. Coin drops use simple denominations; real Quest Items get a discreet golden label. Items pass through a smooth pop, slide and fade rather than suddenly appearing as chat-line text.

The initial September 8 version deliberately allowed only **five ordinary rows**. This constraint preserves screen space and keeps a busy looting moment from turning into a permanent inventory summary.

![Standard loot feed](../Screenshots/loot-feed.png)

## Positioning and timing

The green anchor handle becomes interactable with **/lfeed unlock**. The player drags it to a preferred side of the interface and locks it afterward. Scale ranges **0.6–1.8**; duration ranges **2–20 seconds**; the stack can build **upward or downward**. These settings are account-wide, not per-character.

Hovering an item reveals the game's tooltip while pausing the entire visual stack. That turns a fast notification into inspectable information without a separate details panel. An item whose client cache is still loading falls back to textual/icon placeholders and refreshes when more data arrives.

![Hover item tooltip](../Screenshots/item-tooltip.png)

The gold **Quest Item** label relies on the actual game's tooltip binding text, not on guessing which items a current quest needs.

![Quest item indicator](../Screenshots/quest-item.png)

## Roll details should remain inspectable

Group rolls don't fit in the five-row constraint. They can last longer than a standard loot notification and need room for people and numbers to arrive in stages. The design therefore creates **additional roll rows** that remain while unresolved, show a drawn five-pip die, and keep the winner near that die when known.

Hovering over the dice opens a compact detailed list of Need/Greed/Pass choices and numeric rolls, including waiting/unknown states. The built-in game Need/Greed/Pass dialog remains the place where the player makes a choice; LootFeed is observational only.

Two important UI messages resist false precision:
- Simultaneous identical item drops can be **ambiguous** because item-link chat messages don't identify the unique roll.
- A deadline without a received winner becomes **result unavailable**, which may later update if a real message arrives.

## Behavioral surprises requiring usability review

The source automatically turns on the game's detailed **showLootSpam** option when it was off so the roll details can be received. That has an effect beyond LootFeed's own tiny interface. The optional **/lfeed chat off** also wraps a global chat handler to hide personal loot lines, which may affect interaction with other addons using the same handler.

These are implemented choices, not silently approved future changes. Decide whether a clear opt-in/explanation for the game CVar would better support the creator's direction after an actual in-game test.

## Accessibility tests still outstanding

Test small-scale text contrast, accessible alternatives to color-only rarity distinctions, animation sensitivity, hover-to-pause discoverability, 24px dice-hit targets and busy simultaneous roll displays. No such test was run in this documentation session and no redesigned interface was implemented.

## Verified development pivots

| Git evidence | Design/engineering implementation | Limit |

The code tells us what changed; it cannot prove the full design debate or who typed each implementation line in September.

## Tradeoffs embodied in code

**Ordinary notification limit vs roll expansion:** five regular rows preserve space, but group decisions may need extra simultaneous entries. Both behaviors coexist, rather than truncating important roll status to enforce a universal cap.

**Observed data vs invented certainty:** a chat link identifies an item but not one unique simultaneous roll for identical drops. Ambiguity is displayed explicitly. A timeout lacks a winner and is provisional, so it can be revised by a late authentic message.

**Local prompt vs shared state:** closing the local popup isn't the same as resolving the group. The September 11 correction records this semantic distinction directly in code.

**Chat filtering vs interop:** Vanilla has no modern ChatFrame_AddMessageEventFilter; LootFeed wraps `ChatFrame_OnEvent` to hide only personal item messages. It has a real global-function compatibility surface.

**Data completeness vs control of preferences:** richer roll tooltips require detailed loot spam; the addon sets `showLootSpam=1` if initially off and doesn't restore it. That is a source-visible side effect worth testing and asking the creator about, not something to conceal in a user guide.

**Account-wide preferences, transient events:** display choices carry between characters, while loot and group roll records do not survive reloads. Keeping privacy/lifetime bounded is an observed design outcome, not proof of a specific retention-policy meeting.

**Rename vs continuity:** the general LootFeed name requires migrating old `OctoLootDB`. The helper backs up originals and refuses existing destinations.

# LootFeed — visible content, resource icons and stored preferences

**Creative owner:** Babuni.dev.  
**Scope:** Data and assets displayed by the addon; not a recovered player inventory.

## Visual message types

| UI content | Source data | How it is represented |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Personal item drop | Recognized `CHAT_MSG_LOOT` self-item formats | Item link, item name, cached texture, rarity tint, amount |
| Money | `CHAT_MSG_MONEY` and localized denomination words | Text plus gold/silver/copper icon determined from copper-equivalent amount |
| Quest Item | Actual item binding line of a scanned tooltip | Gold **Quest Item** secondary label |
| Group roll | `START_LOOT_ROLL` + parsed roll chat | Item and dice with players, choices, numbers, status, winner if known |
| Group roll uncertainty | Missing winner or duplicate item-link messages | **Ended (result unavailable)** or explicit ambiguity |
| Preview item feed | `/lfeed test` | Synthetic Linen Cloth, Shadowgem, Peacebloom, Night Watch Shortsword and other examples |
| Preview group roll | `/lfeed testroll` | Synthetic ExampleMage / ExampleRogue; tooltip explicitly calls it a preview |

The addon references the game client's **item/icon textures**, not bundled custom artwork. The dice icon is composed in Lua from a square and five little pips, avoiding a dependency on client-specific dice textures. Rarity coloring comes from the item link's color code.

## Saved data and non-saved state

The manifest declares **SavedVariables: LootFeedDB**. Its current settings are:
- `x, y`: anchor offsets from a defined UIParent anchor.
- `scale`: clamped 0.6–1.8, default 1.
- `duration`: seconds, clamped 2–20, default 6.
- `direction`: up/down, default down.
- `mute`: suppress recognized personal item chat messages via wrapped ChatFrame handler, default false.

**Not saved:** past loot feed messages, queue contents, per-roll participant records, winners, temporary hover/demo state. The phrase “persistent group rolls” historically means visible through the group decision, not stored account-wide.

## Localization and origin of values

Normal self-item templates are drawn from global `LOOT_ITEM_*` strings; rolls are matched using `LOOT_ROLL_*` strings with support for numbered positional placeholders. The quest item binding text references `ITEM_BIND_QUEST`; denominations refer to `GOLD`, `SILVER`, `COPPER`. Text-matching limitations still exist, particularly unusual server formats or positional self-loot strings.

No player's actual group identities, inventories or roll numbers were read or copied into this documentation.

**Client declared in manifest:** World of Warcraft 1.12 / interface 11200 (the project describes 1.12.1)  
**Source:** [MeleeStartAttack.lua](MeleeStartAttack.lua) · [MeleeStartAttack.toc](MeleeStartAttack.toc)  
**Verification:** source and dated Git history reviewed October 26, 2026. No in-game tests performed here.

Melee Start Attack connects **the player's intention to fight** to the game's ordinary auto-attacks. If you press a configured ability as a **Paladin, Warrior or Shaman** against a living, attackable target, the addon can start your basic melee swing **before** the original ability executes—even when a spell is on cooldown or you don't have enough mana or rage. It does not cast abilities for you, select targets, analyze combat performance, or replace the original game action.

Unlike the earlier [WarriorStartAttack](https://github.com/babunidev/WarriorStartAttack), this version has class-specific built-in ability lists, runtime controls and a **learn-the-next-ability** feature that saves additional start/stop behaviors by class.

## Install

Copy both committed files into the AddOns directory with this folder name:

    Interface/AddOns/MeleeStartAttack/
      MeleeStartAttack.toc
      MeleeStartAttack.lua

Restart or reload the game, enable **Melee Start Attack**, and look for the chat message *Melee Start Attack loaded.* A printed load message verifies Lua execution, **not** successful interception of every action API.

The TOC defines SavedVariables **MeleeStartAttackDB**; learned abilities survive reloads/logins, but the simple on/off toggle is **reset to enabled at every load**.

### Recommended attack-state setup

Put WoW's ordinary **Attack** action (from the General spellbook tab) on **any action bar**. The addon scans slots 1–120, remembers an Attack action slot and uses **IsCurrentAction** to check whether basic swings are on. If there is no Attack action present, it uses an in-memory flag updated through combat events and its own calls.

This fallback is less precise: being *in combat* isn't necessarily identical to actively auto-attacking. Repeated presses are **designed** to avoid toggling attacks off, but that behavior has not been verified on an actual client during this audit.

## Supported default ability families

| Class | Built-in start-attack actions |
| --- | --- |
| Paladin — **7 icons** | Seal of Righteousness, Seal of the Crusader, Seal of Light, Seal of Wisdom, Seal of Justice, Seal of Command, Judgement |
| Warrior — **20 icons** | Bloodthirst, Cleave, Demoralizing Shout, Disarm, Execute, Hamstring, Heroic Strike, Intercept, Mortal Strike, Mocking Blow, Overpower, Pummel, Rend, Revenge, Shield Bash, Slam, Sunder Armor, Taunt, Thunder Clap, Whirlwind |
| Shaman — **5 icons** | Earth Shock, Flame Shock, Frost Shock, Stormstrike, **Lightning Strike (custom-ability mapping)** |

The implementation uses **32 class-scoped icon mappings**, not unique spell identifiers. Some ability names are historical source/README labels; the game client must supply matching internal icon textures. Vanilla/custom-client icon collisions or changed textures can produce unexpected matches or omissions.

**Built-in stop-attack exception:** **Warrior Intimidating Shout**. Additional stop actions can be learned for the current class.

## Commands

The primary command aliases are **/meleeattack** and **/msa**:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `/msa` or `/msa toggle` | Toggle automatic start/stop behavior |
| `/msa on` / `/msa off` | Enable or disable automatic triggering **for this session** |
| `/msa status` | Report whether enabled and which auto-attack detection mode is active |
| `/msa learn` or `/msa learn start` | Learn the next recognized ability for **starting** auto-attack |
| `/msa learn stop` | Learn the next recognized ability for **stopping** auto-attack |
| `/msa list` | List learned abilities for your current class |
| `/msa unlearn <spell name>` | Remove the first matching learned **localized spell name** for your class |
| `/msa reset` | Remove all **learned** entries for your current class; built-in icons remain |
| `/start_auto_attack` | Manually start swings if a living hostile/attackable target exists and attack seems off |
| `/stop_auto_attack` | Manually stop swings if attack seems active |

For example, type **/msa learn stop** and press a spell the addon can identify by an internal icon and spellbook name. It will save a **class-specific** entry with `icon`, localized `spellName` and action `stop`. The learned entry follows the ability's **icon** if you move it between action-bar slots. The same press that completes learning also passes through regular start/stop matching; it is not a read-only capture event.

The manual `/start_auto_attack` and `/stop_auto_attack` commands are independent of the automatic enable toggle. The current code also permits learning entries for a class beyond the three with default lists, because learned entries are keyed by whatever class token the client returns; **three classes** is the declared built-in coverage, not a hard runtime restriction for custom learning.

## How ability recognition works

1. Action bar: wrap **UseAction** and query **GetActionTexture**.
2. Spellbook: wrap **CastSpell** and query **GetSpellTexture**.
3. Macros and other addon commands: wrap **CastSpellByName**, find the locally named ability in the spellbook, then compare its **icon**.

These wrappers call the original function after checking the icon. The effect occurs **before** the client can reject a spell for low resources or cooldown. They do not guarantee that a spell succeeded; they do not deliberately auto-cast, queue an ability or change the target.

An icon can be whitelisted and learned at the same time. In the current source **stop takes precedence** over start when a texture is recognized in both lists; learning an opposite behavior does not consistently erase a built-in mapping.

## Persistence and version migrations

MeleeStartAttackDB stores **customAbilities** by **class**, not separate profiles for individual characters. Different characters of the same class using one account SavedVariables table may share learned entries, even if localized names or abilities differ. Earlier version **1.1.2** stored **customStartIcons**; the current code migrates these to records with action **start** and placeholder name **(legacy learned icon)**, then clears the legacy table. To give an old entry a usable name, use learning again on its ability.

No other preferences are saved in the source (in particular, enabled/disabled state and cached Attack-action slot are session-only).

## Known limitations and next checks

- The in-combat fallback does not prove that actual white swings are active, so toggling **AttackTarget()** can be wrong if state drifts.
- Learning is **by icon**, not unique spell ID. Shared icon artwork and same-class custom spells are ambiguous.
- Learning needs a recognizable spellbook name; some macro/custom buttons cannot be identified and may leave learning armed for the next press.
- `/msa off` does not disable the two **manual** start/stop commands.
- Stop/start logic is separate from spell success, mana, rage, GCD and cooldown rules.
- Global function wrappers can conflict with other addons wrapping the same functions, including the related WarriorStartAttack addon.
- True multilingual compatibility was not independently tested; it is the **icon-based design goal**.
- This repo has **no LICENSE file**. Do not assume an open-source license or add one without Babuni.dev's decision.

The [roadmap](ROADMAP.md) gives a reproducible target-client test matrix. Everything above describes current code, **not proven gameplay performance**.
